passages.GK-P0025: The Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters has awarded the 2026 Abel Prize to [1], director emeritus at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn and professor emeritus at the University of Bonn, "for introducing powerful tools in arithmetic geometry and solving long-standing diophantine conjectures by Mordell and Lang." His exceptional achievements unite geometric and arithmetic perspectives and exemplify the power of deep structural insight." In 1983, [1] became famous overnight in the mathematical community when he surprisingly proved Mordell's conjecture using entirely novel methods. The idea behind Mordell's conjecture is thousands of years old. Already the ancient Greek mathematician Diophantus of Alexandria wanted to find out how many integer solutions an equation such as a² + b² = c² has. British rule. The song, written in Sanskritized Bengali, beautifully blends devotion to the nation
with a call for selfless action and sacrifice.

feature it as a reminder of India’s struggle for freedom and the spirit of unity. Celebrating 150

new imperial order. The success at Panipat laid the foundation for the Mughal Empire, which
would eventually become one of the most influential empires in South Asian history. However,
Babur’s position was not immediately secure; he subsequently faced challenges from Rajput
forces under Rana Sanga and Afghan chiefs seeking to restore their influence.

adaptation can sometimes outweigh numerical superiority. Consequently, the First Battle of

When a gravitational wave passes through, it affects the two arms differently as one arm extends, the other contracts,
and vice versa, in a pattern technically referred to as "Differential Arm" motion or differential displacement; this
causes the light waves from the two arms to travel different distances, preventing cancellation, so that the light
escapes through the splitter and strikes the light detector, registering a signal.
A photodetector tracks the timing and motion of the returning laser pulses; this signal, along with corroborating
signals from other detectors in the global network, is then used to study and characterise the gravitational wave
event and trace its cosmic origin.
The measurement requires extraordinary precision as the physical effects of gravitational waves are extremely small
typically causing fractional length changes of approximately 10⁻²¹ over kilometre-scale distances, making LIGO-class
instruments among the most sensitive measurement devices ever constructed.

passages.GK-P0155: Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) operations are a vital part of India's global engagement. As natural and man-made disasters become more frequent and severe, India draws on its extensive disaster management experience to provide timely, coordinated, and well-organized assistance internally and to affected countries. The ability to work in hostile environment, organizational skills and logistics know-hows make the armed forces most suited for HADR operations, and they are often the first responders in the event of any disaster.The objective of HADR is ensuring a "prompt, efficient, coordinated, and responsive" reaction when disasters overwhelm civilian capacities. The Government of India often deploys the Armed Forces to augment national and international relief efforts when civilian capacities are stretched. India's humanitarian aid and disaster relief to our partner countries is focused on providing timely assistance to save lives, alleviate suffering, maintain and protect human dignity during and post disaster. The Indian Army undertakes the deployment of troops for rescue and relief, establishment of field hospitals, restoration of essential infrastructure, and delivery of humanitarian aid. The Indian Navy plays a critical role through evacuation of Indian nationals from abroad, transportation of relief material, and deployment of ships and helicopters for maritime and littoral assistance. The Indian Air Force provides strategic and tactical airlift by ferrying relief supplies, medical teams, and disaster response personnel to affected areas, while also undertaking evacuation and rescue missions. Complementing these efforts, the Indian Coast Guard assists during cyclones, tsunamis, earthquakes, oil platform fires, and flooding in coastal regions, ensuring rapid response and maritime safety.

VII. India recorded 58.85 lakh criminal cases in 2024, a decline from the 62.41 lakh cases reported
in 2028, according to the latest data released on May 6, by the National Crime Records Bureau
(NCRB). The crime rate, measured in terms of cases registered per lakh population, dipped
correspondingly from 448.3 in 2023 to 418.9 in 2024. Of the recorded cases, 35.44 lakh were
registered under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita (BNS), and
23.41 lakh under special and local laws, the report revealed.
This apparent improvement in the overall crime figures ought to be analysed keeping in mind
the complicated reality, with cybercrime, crimes against children and economic offences posing
significant concerns, and the potential impact of legislative reclassification on reflected
numbers.
Cases classified under the ‘hurt' category in IPC sections 325, 326 and 329-335 observed a
major 30.58% drop, reducing from 6.36 lakh to 4.41 lakh in 2024. NCRB, however, clarified
that the dip in cases under ‘hurt or grievous hurt' may be attributed to changes in the BNS,
which replaced the IPC in 2023. Sections of 'hurt or grievous hurt' have been merged while
‘simple hurt' has been reclassified as a non-cognisable offence, meaning it no longer appears in
police registration data. Thus, the fall is likely attributed to legislative change rather than an
actual reduction in number of incidents. [Word Count: 226]

VI.	Human Rights Day is observed every year on [1] to mark the adoption of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) in [2] by the United Nations. This historic declaration
established fundamental rights and freedoms that every individual is entitled to, regardless of
nationality, religion, gender, or social status. It laid the foundation for promoting equality, justice,
and human dignity across the world. The theme for 2025, “[3]” ” emphasizes the importance of
ensuring that basic rights, such as access to education, healthcare, food, and safety, are integral to
daily life for everyone.
In India, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established in [4] under the
Protection of Human Rights Act as an independent statutory body to protect and promote human
rights. The NHRC operates according to the [5], which guide national human rights institutions
worldwide. Its functions include monitoring violations, investigating complaints, recommending
corrective measures, and spreading awareness about human rights. The commission plays a
crucial role in protecting vulnerable sections of society and ensuring accountability in governance.
Human Rights Day reminds citizens and governments of their responsibility to uphold human
dignity and justice. It is a day to reflect on the rights that are essential for freedom, equality, and
well-being, and to take collective action to ensure that these rights are respected in everyday life.
passages.GK-P0159:
X.	It is impossible not to smile darkly when the results of a G2 summit are discrepant readouts:
It seems that presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping cannot agree on what was agreed on
during their recent talks. The good news: They seem not to be colluding to divide up the world
into new spheres of influence. But global instability is not about to diminish.
Today, international trade is increasingly shaped by geopolitical rivalries, national security
concerns, and strategic competition among major powers. Governments are no longer viewing
trade solely as a means of economic exchange; it is also being used as an instrument of foreign
policy and national strategy. This shift has exposed the limitations of a trade framework that
often treats economic issues in isolation from broader political realities.
At the same time, several longstanding concerns of developing countries remain unresolved.
Questions relating to equitable development, market access, and the unequal distribution of
gains from globalization continue to feature prominently in international trade discussions.
Meanwhile, new challenges have emerged, including concerns about supply-chain
vulnerabilities, technological dependence, cybersecurity risks, and the environmental
consequences of economic growth. These issues often extend beyond the traditional mandate of
trade institutions but nevertheless influence trade relations in significant ways.
Many observers argue that if the WTO is to remain effective, it must acknowledge the political
forces shaping global commerce rather than treating them as external factors. Recognizing
differences in national priorities, accommodating diverse developmental needs, and
encouraging more flexible forms of cooperation may help the organization adapt to a rapidly
changing world. Ultimately, the future of the multilateral trading system may depend on its
ability to balance economic objectives with the political realities that increasingly influence
international trade.
Source: Amrita Narlikar, For WTO to Matter, It Needs to Recognise Politics Behind Trade,

passages.GK-P0238: In a historic and unprecedented moment, the Government of India today marked the 200th Birth Anniversary of Mahatma Jyotiba Phule with solemn tributes at the Parliament House Complex, signifying the nation's highest institutional recognition of one of its greatest social reformers. GENERAL KNOWLEDGE

I. The view that artificial intelligence (AI) can pose an existential threat to humankind using technologies like
nuclear weapons has been around for some years now. Last year, after examining such threats and risks,
one study from the Rand Corporation, a global policy think-tank, argued that such risks could not be ruled out.

The study also went on to identify four capabilities that it said AI will have to possess in order to pose an
existential threat: “(i) integration with key cyber-physical systems, (ii) the ability to survive without human
maintainers, (iii) the objective to cause human extinction, and (iv) the ability to persuade or deceive humans to
avoid detection.”
But recent developments, including the conflicts in West and South Asia and in Eastern Europe, have kept
concerns that mix nuclear weapons and AI alive.

In the absence of a specific treaty to address such a threat, on July 16, a group of Nobel laureates, AI scientists,
religious leaders, and other luminaries signed the so-called ‘Rome Declaration for an Unarmed and Disarming
Peace’. The Declaration calls for an international treaty to ban autonomous systems from accessing nuclear
launches while emphasising that the threat is also not so far-fetched.

Inspired by Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which issued a “clarion call” to protect human
dignity against technological overreach, the Declaration can be read more as a nudge than as an impactful push
for a treaty. At present, there is no consensus among countries on what such a treaty should cover or even on
banning AI with autonomous capabilities on the war front.
Source- https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/rome-declaration-convergent-perils-luminaries-human-

The record was adopted in Montreux, Switzerland, in 1990, and it identifies Ramsar Sites that require priority
conservation attention at the national or international level.
Two Indian wetlands are currently in the record, namely Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan and Loktak Lake in
Manipur.
Chilika Lake in Odisha was placed in the record but was later removed from it.

India's Ramsar network has grown to 100 sites spread across 28 states and union territories, an expansion from an
earlier recorded national total of 85 sites.
An earlier assessment recorded India's Ramsar wetlands as spanning about 11,000 square kilometres, roughly 10
per cent of the country's total wetland area, across 18 states.
Tamil Nadu has the highest number of Ramsar Sites among Indian states, with the count recorded at 20.
The Sundarban Wetland in West Bengal is the largest Ramsar Site in India at 4,230 square kilometres.
It is followed by the Kazhuveli Bird Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu at 1,513 square kilometres, the Vembanad-Kol Wetland
in Kerala at 1,512.5 square kilometres, Chilika Lake in Odisha at 1,165 square kilometres, the Satkosia Gorge in
Odisha at 981.97 square kilometres, and Kolleru Lake in Andhra Pradesh at 901 square kilometres.

passages.GK-P0332:
VU. India and the European Union concluded a Free Trade Agreement (FTA), paving the way for strong
geoeconomic relations between the two. However, the deal awaits ratification by the European
Parliament, EU member states, and India before entering into force. Ratification appears likely, given
the strategic incentives on both sides to diversify economic and geopolitical partnerships. But the
process may be protracted and politically contested, GeoQuant, a unit of Fitch Solutions, has said.
Some members of the EU may raise concerns over sensitive sectors and regulatory standards. Domestic
political pressures can also play a role in the ratification of the FTA, as with past EU trade agreements.
Fitch unit said that parliamentary scrutiny could also slow the ratification progress in India,
particularly where stakeholders question the enforceability of FDI provisions or seek further revisions
on carbon-related measures and agricultural market access. The formal signing of the India-EU free
trade agreement will take place after legal scrubbing, Commerce Secretary had said earlier, following
which the deal will move towards ratification on both sides. GeoQuant's risk chart on India's
Investment/Trade Policy continues to fall, supported by the conclusion of a landmark Free Trade
Agreement with the EU.
The trade agreement will be one of the most comprehensive trade pacts either side has signed. This
ends nearly two decades of stop-start talks between the two economies. The India-EU trade pact is
expected to benefit sectors such as machinery, automotive, pharmaceuticals, and financial services,
while granting Indian exports, including textiles, engineering goods, and spices, improved access to the
EU market. It would also foster deeper integration in services, investment flows, and labour mobility.
The commerce minister said that both sides chose to defer or ring-fence politically and economically
sensitive issues to arrive at what he described as a balanced outcome. www.lawpreptutorial.com

passages.GK-P0333:
SECTION II
V.	With global temperatures at near-record levels and El Nifio set to return, governments,
businesses, communities, and individuals across the world today marked World Environment
Day, sounding the alarm on the need to urgently address climate change. This year,
Azerbaijan hosted the official commemoration of World Environment Day.
Extreme heat is one of the deadliest and fastest-growing climate threats to lives, livelihoods,
and economies. The overshoot of the Paris Agreement goal of 1.5°C now almost inevitable and
impacts escalating, cutting emissions and adapting to rising risks.
This World Environment Day, warning signals are everywhere. The past eleven years have
been the eleven hottest on record. The world is heading for a temporary overshoot above 1.5
degrees, UN Secretary-General Anténio Guterres stated in his message for World
Environment Day 2026. Our task is to make that overshoot as small, as short, and as safe as
possible — and rapidly bring temperatures back down.
That means slashing emissions. Accelerating a just transition away from fossil fuels and
towards renewables — the only sustainable path to lower costs and to real energy security.
Cutting methane — one of the fastest, cheapest ways to limit near-term warming. Protecting
forests, land, and seas. Helping communities adapt to the devastating impacts already here.
And it means fulfilling climate finance promises to developing countries — to save lives, protect
livelihoods, and strengthen economies, he added. This is the moment to act — for our
environment and for our future. As our planet continues to face the devastating impacts of
climate change, the science is clear. [Word Count: 252]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.unep.org/news-and-
stories /press-release/planet-swelters-world-environment-day-2026-focuses-urgent-climate

VII. When US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping concluded their summit
at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People last week, much was riding on the G2 framework that
Trump had boasted about in October last year before returning to China and repeating it.
India’s silence carried new weight, and this was not the comfortable ambiguity of the Cold
War, when equidistance between superpowers was a moral posture. This was the anxious
silence of a country that has staked its technological future on partnership with Washington,
while knowing that the neighbour on its northern border now sits across from America as an
equal.
The stakes are sharper than at any previous US-China summit because the technology gap
that once made India’s diplomatic geometry manageable has closed. The recently released
Stanford Institute for Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence’s 2026 AI Index Report found that
China has nearly erased America’s lead. As of March 2026, the US advantage in frontier model
performance stood at just 2.7 per cent. Russell Wald, HAI’s executive director, has warned that
policymakers globally are failing to understand the technologies they are being pushed to
govern. This also applies to India, where the AI ecosystem is still playing catch-up, and the
IndiaAI Mission at $1.2 billion amounts to what a single American AI company spends in six
months. India’s ambitions are laudable, but its resourcing is not.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from
https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns /xi-trump-us-china-tech-race-india-modi-

Paving the way for the mother of all defence deals, defence minister Rajnath Singh- lead defence
acquisition council (DAC) on Thursday approved the acquisition of 114 Rafale fighter jets from
France, just 5 days ahead of the arrival of French president Emmanuel Macron in India. Though
the ministry did not provide the exact cost of 114 Rafale jets, the proposed government-to-
government deal is expected to be worth around 3.25 lakh crore, which, when signed with France’s
Dassault Aviation after final cost negotiations and the cabinet’s approval, will make it India's
biggest defence deal since independence. About 20 of the multi-role fighters will be brought in fly-
away condition and are expected to be added to the IAF fleet by 2030, while the rest will be
manufactured with Dassault-HAL collaboration in India. The DAC nod for more Rafale jets is the
government's biggest vote of confidence on the French multirole fighter, which IAF vice-chief
described just a day before as the “operation Sindoor hero” for its precision strikes on Pakistan’s
terror infrastructure and military bases. The confrontation with Pakistan saw a systematic
campaign by social media influencers, suspected to be backed by Pakistan and China, to discredit
the French aircraft amid unconfirmed reports of the loss of the French fighter jets. The IAF
currently operates 36 Rafale jets, and the Indian Navy last year placed an order for 26 of its naval
variants.

VIL. India’s rural employment framework has been central to addressing livelihood insecurity and
asset creation in rural areas. Over time, policy debates have emerged regarding the efficiency,
fiscal sustainability and developmental impact of existing employment guarantee models.
Concerns related to non-durable asset creation, labour market distortions and rising expenditure
have prompted discussions on restructuring rural employment schemes.
The proposed approach under the VB—-G RAM G framework seeks to integrate employment
generation with long-term infrastructure development and livelihood enhancement. Emphasis is
placed on creating durable assets aligned with national priorities such as water security, rural
connectivity and climate resilience. Planning mechanisms are designed to operate through local
institutions while remaining aligned with broader infrastructure strategies.
Fiscal restructuring forms an important component, with a shift towards defined allocations and
shared responsibility between the Centre and States. Digital platforms and data-driven planning
tools aim to improve transparency, monitoring and convergence with other development
programmes. Seasonal flexibility in implementation is intended to reduce conflicts with
agricultural labour demand.
The framework reflects a broader shift from welfare-oriented employment provision to
productivity-linked rural development. At the same time, its effectiveness depends on institutional
capacity, coordination across governance levels and the ability to balance social protection with
economic efficiency in rural policy design.

The Principle of Open Justice:
The court acknowledged that the principle of open justice requires judicial records to remain available and
accessible as a foundational guarantee of transparency in the functioning of the justice system.
However, the court held that open justice does not mandate that a private individual's name must function as a
permanent retrieval key through commercial search engines.
Balancing Open Justice with Personal Dignity
The Court's Reasoning:
The court observed that open justice was conceived to ensure that the judicial process is accessible and fully
transparent, but that it would be incongruous if this same principle served as justification for the perpetual and
indiscriminate amplification of a person's worst travails with legal processes.
The court drew a distinction between maintaining accessible judicial records as a matter of institutional
transparency and the commercial amplification by search engine algorithms of an individual's association with those
records across the open internet.
Who May Seek Relief:
Individuals who have been acquitted, discharged, or whose cases have been quashed are eligible to seek de-indexing
of related judicial records under the framework laid down by the court.
Parties to matrimonial disputes, persons whose proceedings have been settled, and persons whose names appeared
only incidentally in judicial records also fall within the scope of eligible applicants.

What PPI Measures:
The PPI measures the average change over time in the prices received by domestic producers for the goods and
services they sell, tracking inflation from the producer's perspective before price changes reach consumers.
While the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures what consumers pay at the retail level, PPI measures what
manufacturers and service providers receive for their output at the factory-gate level.
PPI serves as an early indicator of inflationary pressures and helps assess how input costs are transmitted to the final
prices of products.
Three Pillars of the PPI Framework:
Input PPI measures the change in prices of the raw materials, goods, and services that industries purchase to
manufacture their final products, compiled using the Purchaser's Price; an example would be the cost of steel, rubber,
and electricity for a car manufacturer.
Output PPI measures the change in prices that industries receive for the final goods and services they produce,
compiled on the basis of Basic Price; an example would be the factory price of a finished car.
Service PPI specifically tracks price changes in the service sector, which constitutes over 50 per cent of India's GDP
but was excluded entirely from the WPI.
In the first phase, it covers seven services: Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension
Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom.
It is compiled on a quarterly basis and on the basis of Basic Price.
Additional service sectors are planned for inclusion in subsequent phases.

V.	The European Union has officially joined Pax Silica, a U.S.-led international initiative
designed to strengthen the security of global supply chains that support artificial intelligence
(AI) and advanced semiconductor technologies. The decision reflects growing cooperation
among like-minded nations seeking to reduce vulnerabilities in critical technology sectors and
ensure uninterrupted access to essential resources.
Pax Silica focuses on building resilient supply chains for AI by promoting collaboration in
areas such as critical minerals, energy resources, advanced manufacturing, semiconductor
production, and AI model development. As AI becomes increasingly important for economic
growth, national security, and technological innovation, participating countries aim to reduce
their dependence on unstable or concentrated sources of key materials and technologies.
The European Commission confirmed its participation through its spokesperson, highlighting
the bloc's commitment to working closely with trusted international partners on Al-related
supply chain security. The Netherlands had also joined the initiative earlier, further
strengthening European participation in the alliance.
The initiative, led by the U.S. State Department, seeks to encourage greater coordination
among partner countries to safeguard critical technologies against future disruptions. By
promoting secure and diversified supply chains, Pax Silica aims to support long-term
innovation while ensuring reliable access to the resources required for developing next-
generation AI systems.
The EU's decision to become part of Pax Silica marks another step in expanding international
cooperation on emerging technologies. As geopolitical competition and _ technological
dependence continue to shape global policy, such partnerships are expected to play an
important role in strengthening economic resilience and supporting the responsible growth of
the global AI ecosystem.
Source: Reuters. (2026, June 25). EU joins U.S.-led 'Pax Silica' on securing AI, chip supply
chains.
passages.GK-P0347: The Indian women's compound team, comprising veteran Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Madhura Dhamangaonkar and Pragati, won the gold medal at the Archery World Cup 2026 Stage 1 in [1]. The top-seeded Indian archery team defeated the USA's Paige Pearce, Olivia Dean and Alexis Ruiz 233-232 in the final. India trailed 117-114 at the end of the second set, and reduced it to a point at 174-173 in the next. Riding on four Xs and two 10s, the Indian team overturned the deficit in the fourth and final set to secure the country's only medal at the season- opening leg of the 2026 Archery World Cup. The USA women's compound archery team, seeded third, came into the contest with a significant pedigree, with all three archers having medalled at the World Archery Championships. Earlier, world No. 3 Jyothi Surekha, Madhura Dhamangaonkar, the 2025 Shanghai World Cup gold medallist, and the 22-year-old Pragati had beaten fourth seeds Turkiye 233- 230 in the semi-finals after a 235-234 win over Denmark.Having topped the qualification round with a combined score of 2074, India received a bye in the opening round. Pragati was India's standout performer in qualification, shooting 694 to finish sixth overall in a 54- archer field. Jyothi Surekha, the reigning Asian Games champion, was 10th with 691, while Madhura Dhamangaonkar placed 15th with 689. India missed out on a medal in the compound mixed team event, which will make its Olympic debut at LA 2028, with Ojas Deotale and Pragati losing to the USA's Alexis Ruiz and Stephan Hansen 155-154 in the bronze-medal match. In the individual events, Jyothi was the top-performing Indian archer. She beat the reigning world champion and No.1 Andrea Becerra of Mexico and world No. 2 Ella Gibson of Great Britain was beaten by local favourite Dafne Quintero 149-143 in the quarter-finals.

IV.	Sunlight floods the room from the bay window, reflects off the wide, honey-coloured
floorboards and casts an emerald glow over the perforate leaves of a monstera shaped like a
cloud. Its stems brush the back of a Scandinavian armchair, an open magazine left face-down
on the seat. The red of that magazine cover, the plant’s brilliant green, the petrol blue of the
upholstery and the pale ochre floor stand out against the white walls, their chalky tone picked
up again in the pale rug that just creeps into the frame.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The next picture is of the building’s exterior, an Art Nouveau apartment block with acanthus
leaf and citrus fruit cornices. The white render is all but invisible under layers of fluorescent
graffiti, tattered posters and peeling paint. On the first floor, you can scarcely make out the
stucco gables beneath the grime. The combination of turn-of-the-century luxury and raw
modern grittiness lends a feeling of freedom and decadence, with a hint of eroticism. Some of
the windows are boarded up with faded chipboard, but in others there are plants and string
lights. An ivy cascades from a balcony onto the street below.
Source: An extract from Perfection by Vincenzo Latronico, translated by Sophie Hughes

V.	It's official. The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), formed less than four years ago, has won
Nepal's general elections by a landslide. The party's candidate, Balendra Shah, a former
rapper, is set to become the next prime minister of the Himalayan nation
Shah’s RSP won 182 seats in the 275-member parliament, Nepal’s election commission said on
Thursday, 12 March. This is the largest majority of any party in more than six decades, the
officials said.
The March 5 election was the Himalayan nation's first vote since demonstrations against
corruption last September led by Gen Z protesters that killed 77 people and toppled the
government led by Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli.
"If everything goes well, we can expect that it can give a stable government for five years,"
constitutional expert Purna Man Shakya told Reuters, referring to splits over dividing up the
spoils of office that doomed prior majority governments.
The RSP is led by former television personality Rabi Lamichhane, who serves as the party's
chairman. On 16 June 2022, Lamichhane resigned as managing director of Galaxy 4K
television and announced that he would contest the 2022 general elections for a seat in the
House of Representatives.
On 21 June 2022, he announced the formation of RSP. The party was formally registered with
the Election Commission on 1 July 2022, with Rabi Lamichhane as the founding president,
and a bell inside a circle as its election symbol.

VII. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed Indian smartphone companies,
including manufacturers and importers, to pre-install the state-developed cybersecurity
application called Sanchar Saathi. The DoT directive, issued on November 28 under the
Telecommunication Cybersecurity Amendment Rules, 2025, sparked criticism over privacy and
surveillance issues. The diktat effectively meant that users had no say in whether they wanted to
use the app, and no option to remove it if their phone came preinstalled with it. For this to work in
practice, the app will almost certainly need system level or root level access, similar to carrier or
OEM system apps, so that it cannot be disabled. That design choice erodes the protections that
normally prevent one app from peering into the data of others, and turns Sanchar Saathi into a
permanent, non-consensual point of access sitting inside the operating system of every Indian
smartphone user. This is the first time the government has issued a directive mandating the
installation of a state-backed application on phones. While such a move would be unusual in most
Western democracies, it is not entirely without precedent. Besides, when the Telecommunications
Act was being finalised in 2023, several concerns were raised that the law might be broad and
cover online platforms as well. While the government had then said that no such overlaps would
happen, the telecom cybersecurity rules, which draw their powers from the Telecom Act, are now
being used to issue directions to tech companies.
[Sanchar Saathi App Controversy; Word Count: 241]

VII. Developments in a high-profile criminal case again brought attention to the principles
governing bail and appellate review in India. The Supreme Court was approached after orders
passed by a lower court were challenged, prompting scrutiny of factors such as the gravity of
allegations, stage of trial, rights of the accused, and protection of victims and witnesses. The
episode reignited debate on how courts balance personal liberty with societal interests,
particularly in serious offences. Legal experts reiterated that bail is a matter of judicial
discretion guided by precedent rather than automatic entitlement. They also highlighted the
Court’s power to stay orders of other courts where necessary to prevent injustice. The
discussion surrounding the case contributed to public understanding of constitutional
safeguards, rule of law, and the layered appeal structure within India’s criminal justice system.

According to a press note by the Ministry of External Affairs, the launch will be made by External Affairs
Minister S. Jaishankar who is currently travelling in the Gulf region and will reach New York city on July 10 for
the official ceremony that will be crucial from the point of view of India’s leadership position in the Global
South. The bid for the non-permanent seat at the UNSC comes at a time when the world is witnessing several
disruptive events such as the crisis in the Gulf following the U.S.-Israel war on Iran that has disrupted energy
and fertilizer trade with much of the world, including the Global South. The bid will also require substantial
diplomatic mobilisation by India as Tajikistan will be the other candidate for the seat meant for the Asia-Pacific
region. While India has received support from countries such as Fiji, United States, Austria and Sri Lanka, it
will have to do considerable diplomatic heavy lifting as Tajikistan has already secured the support of the OIC
bloc that consists of 57 member-states of the United Nations. That apart, both countries are members of the
SCO that will hold the next summit meeting in Kyrgyzstan, adding a special significance to the summit from
the point of view of UNSC ambitions of India and Tajikistan.

This week he is visiting Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, having visited Qatar during the weekend. He will reach
New York city for extensive consultations with India’s partners at the UN. While India has been advocating a
reform at the UNSC and also has been championing the needs of the Global South, recent trends however have
not gone according to the plans. Earlier in May, India postponed the India-Africa Forum Summit that was to be
held during May 28-31 citing the Ebola outbreak in multiple countries in Africa.

He was repeatedly imprisoned and exiled by the Shah’s regime for his anti-monarchist sermons and
writings, which promoted Islamic governance and denounced Western imperialism.
His activism made him one of the key religious figures during the Islamic Revolution of 1979, which
overthrew the monarchy and established the Islamic Republic of Iran.
After the revolution, Khamenei became a prominent figure in the new Islamic Republic and held several
key positions.
In 1981, after the assassination of President Mohammad-Ali Rajai, Khamenei was elected as the third

consider setting up regional Courts of Appeal so that the Supreme Court can focus mainly on
constitutional matters.

increasing the number of judges must be accompanied by wider judicial reforms to effectively
tackle delays and pendency in the justice delivery system.

rotates monthly among all 15 members; India held the Presidency in 2022.

membership may participate in deliberations without a vote when their interests are directly affected.

rule. Over the next two decades, most colonies in Asia and Africa emerged as free, independent
nations. They were, however, overburdened by poverty and a lack of resources, and their
economies and societies were handicapped by long periods of colonial rule.

countries. They were not equipped to cope with the challenge of poverty and lack of development
in the former colonies. But as Europe and Japan rapidly rebuilt their economies, they grew less
dependent on the IMF and the World Bank. Thus, from the late 1950s, the Bretton Woods
institutions began to shift their attention more towards developing countries.

out of poverty, they came under the guidance of international agencies dominated by the former
colonial powers. Even after many years of decolonisation, the former colonial powers still
controlled vital resources such as minerals and land in many of their former colonies.

passages.GK-P0489: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 criminalises paper leakage, unauthorised assistance, tampering, and organised cheating in public examinations conducted by scheduled authorities. The Act presently provides three to five years’ imprisonment and a fine up to ₹10 lakh for ordinary offences. Organised crime attracts at least five years’ imprisonment and a fine of at least ₹1 crore. In July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to strengthen the law. According to the draft reported as circulated to MPs, ordinary punishment would rise to five to ten years with a fine up to ₹50 lakh, while organised crime would attract at least seven years and a fine of at least ₹10 crore. The proposal also contemplates a Special Task Force, a two-month investigation target, designated Sessions Courts, trial within three months after filing of the charge sheet, and transfer of pending cases. Cabinet approval does not enact these changes. They become law only after the legislative process, presidential assent, and any required commencement step.
passages.GK-P0490: Mission Drishti, the world's first OptoSAR satellite developed by Bengaluru based space startup GalaxEye has been successfully launched on May 3, 2026 aboard a Falcon 9 by SpaceX from Vandenberg, California. Weighing 190 kilograms, Mission Drishti is India's largest privately developed Earth observation satellite. "It is the first satellite globally to integrate Electro-Optical (EO) and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors into a single operational platform, enabling all-weather, day-and-night imaging capabilities. This integrated approach addresses long-standing limitations of conventional systems and enables more reliable and consistent data acquisition across diverse environmental conditions," GalaxEye said. "Mission Drishti marks our first mission and the culmination of over five years of sustained R&D to develop this breakthrough technology. With the satellite now successfully in orbit, our immediate focus is on completing its commissioning. As we move through this phase, we are already witnessing strong global interest in the differentiated datasets enabled by our OptoSAR payload." said Suyash Singh, Founder & CEO, GalaxEye. Following its successful deployment and commissioning initial imagery is expected to be delivered to customers in the coming weeks. GalaxEye said that the satellite has already generated significant interest from government and commercial stakeholders internationally, seeking access to high-quality, high-frequency Earth observation data. On the successful launch, Dr. Pawan Goenka, Chairman, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe) said that the sustained effort over the last five to six years on confidence-building, capacity-building and the commercialisation of India's private space technology ecosystem is now showing tangible results. "Mission Drishti by GalaxEye is a fine example of this - the world's first OptoSAR satellite from an Indian private player. As more Indian space companies demonstrate their capabilities through real missions and engagement with global customers, confidence in India's space ecosystem will continue to strengthen, creating greater demand both in India and overseas. I compliment the GalaxEye team on this important milestone and wish them continued success," said Dr. Goenka. Mission Drishti is a dual-use Earth observation Satellite, supporting use cases across defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring, and infrastructure planning. The satellite is expected to complement India's broader initiatives, including the active 29 Earth Observation satellites outlined in ISRO's recent annual report.

IV.	The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 took the world by surprise and marked a major
turning point in global politics. With the end of one of the two superpowers, the United States
emerged as the dominant force in international relations. This period is often seen as the
beginning of US hegemony, although some of its foundations had already been laid after the
end of the Second World War in 1945. However, the US did not immediately act as a
hegemonic power; it gradually assumed this role over time.
A significant event that highlighted the growing dominance of the US was the First Gulf War.
In August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait and annexed it. After diplomatic efforts failed, the
United Nations authorised military action to liberate Kuwait. This was a crucial decision,
especially after years of Cold War deadlock.
The US President George H.W. Bush described this moment as the emergence of a "new world
order." A coalition of around 660,000 troops from 34 countries was formed, but the operation
was largely dominated by the US. Led by American General Norman Schwarzkopf, nearly 75%
of the forces belonged to the US.
Despite strong claims by Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, Iraqi forces were swiftly defeated and
forced to withdraw from Kuwait, reinforcing US military supremacy.

VII. Air pollution across Delhi-NCR pushed into another dangerous stretch this week, with several
stations logging AQI readings above 600. The spike also left many neighbouring regions, including
Noida, Greater Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram and Faridabad, inside the severe bracket and raised
immediate concerns about exposure and health risks for residents. Governments in Delhi-NCR
must act in accordance with the GRAP mechanism as air pollution levels rise through various
stages. There are four stages in GRAP, each linked to the Air Quality Index (AQI) at the time.
When the AQI is 201-300 or the air quality is categorised as ‘poor’, GRAP-I or the first stage of the
framework kicks in. Stage I focuses on early curbs. Stopping open waste burning, removing coal
use in small eateries, and deploying local checks on dust and emissions. The second stage is
invoked when the air quality becomes ‘very poor’ or the AQI is 301-400. Stage II brings in stronger
steps: a halt on diesel generator sets except for essential services, higher parking fees, dust-control
sprinkling, and tighter movement for BS-IV diesel vehicles. GRAP-III is arrived at when the
pollution is ‘severe’ or AQI is 401-450. Stage III restrictions continue across NCR. This includes: A
ban on non-essential construction - piling, excavation, demolition, prohibition on BS-III and BS-IV
diesel vehicles across Delhi-NCR, monitoring of mines, stone crushers and diesel-run machinery
and possible closure of lower classes in schools. Penalties for repeated violations. During GRAP-
IV, conditions enter the ‘severet+’ range. A host of measures are being taken by the Delhi-NCR
administrations under GRAP-IV.

X.	Effective Wednesday, every petrol pump in India will dispense petrol blended with 20%
ethanol (E20), following a government mandate announced last month. The nationwide rollout
pushes ahead even as most vehicles on the road are not built for the fuel, raising concerns over
efficiency and engine wear.
The transition marks a significant milestone in India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP)
Programme, which aims to increase the use of domestically produced biofuels. Ethanol,
primarily produced from sugarcane, maize, and damaged food grains, helps lower greenhouse
gas emissions while reducing the country's dependence on imported fossil fuels. The
programme also provides an additional source of income for farmers and supports the rural
economy.
However, the rollout has also raised concerns among vehicle owners. Most vehicles
manufactured in recent years are designed to operate on E20 fuel, but older vehicles may
experience a slight reduction in fuel efficiency because ethanol contains less energy than
conventional petrol. Automobile manufacturers recommend that consumers verify whether
their vehicles are E20-compatible before regular use. Experts also advise following
manufacturer guidelines for maintenance to ensure optimum engine performance and
longevity.
Despite these challenges, the government views ethanol blending as a long-term solution for
achieving energy independence and environmental sustainability. By encouraging the use of
renewable fuels and reducing reliance on imported crude oil, the E20 initiative represents an
important step towards cleaner transportation and a more resilient energy sector while
supporting India's broader climate and economic objectives.
Source: Mint, "E20 petrol rollout: What it means for your vehicle." Published 1 April 2026.

IV.	In the bustling streets of New York City, a young woman named Elena found herself caught
between two worlds. On one hand, there was her career as a promising architect, where every
project was a step toward professional success. On the other, there was her deep yearning for
something more—something beyond the glass-and-steel skyscrapers she designed. For years, she
had lived by the rigid rules of ambition and competition, but recently, an unusual sense of
dissatisfaction had started to cloud her vision.
It wasn’t the kind of dissatisfaction that could be solved with a raise or a promotion. Elena was
tired of designing buildings that were impressive on paper but lifeless in spirit. She longed for
creative freedom, the kind that could only be found in art. Her sketches, once filled with geometric
precision, now overflowed with swirling lines and bold, vibrant colors—shapes that had no purpose
except to express an emotion she couldn’t name.
One evening, after a long day at the office, Elena walked to a nearby park. She sat by the fountain,
letting the sound of the water soothe her mind. As the sky began to darken, she took out her
sketchbook and began to draw without thinking. She didn’t care whether it was perfect or
practical. For the first time in years, Elena felt alive.
The city’s chaos seemed distant now. In the stillness of the park, she realized something profound:
It wasn’t success she sought, but authenticity. The answer had always been within her, waiting for
her to stop chasing after an ideal and embrace what truly mattered. And with that realization,
Elena began to feel a sense of peace she had never known before.
passages.GK-P0504: The United Nations is negotiating a Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation together with two early protocols. The fifth negotiating session, which opened in New York on 3 August 2026, is the first at which member states are expected to work across concrete draft legal language in all three workstreams. One protocol concerns income from cross-border services in an increasingly digitalized economy; the other concerns the prevention and resolution of tax disputes. The framework convention is intended to supply wider objectives, principles, governance, and cooperation machinery. The process responds partly to disagreements over which countries should tax profits when a business can earn revenue from customers in a jurisdiction without maintaining the traditional physical presence there. Residence countries, source countries, and market jurisdictions may claim different connections to the same income. Coordination can reduce both double taxation and non-taxation, but states disagree over the allocation of taxing rights. The committee is scheduled to complete final texts for General Assembly consideration in 2027. Those negotiations do not themselves impose a tax in India. Article 265 requires authority of law for any Indian tax, while Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws implementing treaties and international decisions. A negotiated text, General Assembly consideration, state consent to be bound, entry into force, and domestic implementation must therefore be kept legally distinct.
passages.GK-P0505: The passage of the Union Budget through Parliament involves a meticulous multi-stage constitutional procedure. Under Article 112, the President causes to be laid before both Houses the 'Annual Financial Statement'. Following general discussion, the Lok Sabha votes on the 'Demands for Grants'. Due to time constraints, on the final allotted day for voting, the Speaker applies the 'guillotine' procedure, putting all remaining undiscussed demands to vote simultaneously. Once demands are passed, the Appropriation Bill is introduced under Article 114 to authorize expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India. Finally, the Finance Bill containing taxation proposals is passed. Money Bills, defined strictly under Article 110, require Presidential recommendation and Lok Sabha supremacy; Rajya Sabha can only delay a Money Bill for 14 days.

VUI. Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada River in Gujarat. This is one of the largest
water resource projects of India covering four states—Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and
Rajasthan. The Sardar Sarovar project would meet the requirement of water in drought-prone and
desert areas. Sardar Sarovar Project will provide irrigation facilities to 18.45 lakh hectare of land,
covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. It will also irrigate 2,46,000 hectare of land in the
strategic desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan and 37,500 hectare in the tribal hilly
tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat is drought
prone while entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone. Assured water supply will soon make
this area drought proof.
However, in recent years, multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny
and opposition for a variety of reasons. Regulating and damming of rivers affect their natural flow
causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting
in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for the rivers’ aquatic life. Dams also fragment rivers
making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. The reservoirs that are
created on the floodplains also submerge the existing vegetation and soil leading to its
decomposition over a period of time.www.lawpreptutorial.com
These floods have not only devastated life and property but also caused extensive soil erosion.
Sedimentation also meant that the flood plains were deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, further
adding on to the problem of land degradation. It was also observed that the multi purpose projects
induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution resulting from

excessive use of water. Irrigation has also changed the cropping pattern of many regions with
farmers shifting to water intensive and commercial crops. This has great ecological consequences
like salinisation of the soil. Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana has been started which
ensures access to some means to protective irrigation for all agricultural farms in the country,
thus bringing much desired rural prosperity. Some of the broad objectives of this programme are
to enhance the physical access of water on the farm and expand cultivable area under assured
irrigation (har khet ko pani), improve on-farm water use efficiency to reduce wastage and increase
availability both in duration and extent, irrigation and other water saving technologies (per drop
more crop) and introduce sustainable water conservation practices, etc.
Source: NCERT Class X, Contemporary World

IX.	The concept of power-sharing has developed as a response to the earlier belief in the concentration
of political power in the hands of a single person or group. Traditionally, it was assumed that
centralized power allowed governments to take quick decisions and enforce them effectively.
Distributing power, it was feared, would weaken authority and slow down governance. However,
with the rise of democratic systems, these ideas have changed significantly. Democracy rests on
the principle that all political power originates from the people. In a democratic setup, citizens
govern themselves through institutions of self-government, and due respect is given to the
diversity of opinions, interests, and social groups present in society. To ensure meaningful
participation and representation, political power must be shared among a wide section of the
population.
Modern democracies adopt various power-sharing arrangements. One important form is the
horizontal distribution of power among the three main organs of government: the legislature,
executive, and judiciary. Although these institutions operate at the same level, they are assigned
different responsibilities and powers. This separation ensures that no single organ can dominate
the others or misuse authority. Each institution acts as a check on the powers of the others,
creating a balance known as the system of checks and balances. For instance, the executive is
accountable to the legislature, while the judiciary can review the actions of both the legislature
and the executive to ensure they follow constitutional principles.
Another significant form of power-sharing is vertical distribution, where authority is divided
among different levels of government. This includes a central or federal government for the entire
country and state or regional governments for different provinces. In India, this system exists
between the Union Government and the State Governments, with the Constitution clearly
defining their respective powers. This principle is also extended to local levels of governance such
as municipalities and panchayats, allowing citizens to participate directly in decision-making at
the grassroots level.
Power can also be shared among different social groups, including religious, linguistic, and ethnic
communities. Such arrangements help ensure fair representation of minorities and socially
weaker sections in governance. Examples include Belgium’s community government and India’s
system of reserved constituencies, which aim to prevent marginalization and foster social
harmony.
Lastly, power-sharing occurs through political parties, pressure groups, and social movements.
Competition among political parties ensures that power does not remain concentrated in one hand.
Coalition governments, formed by alliances of parties, are a direct example of shared power.
Additionally, interest groups influence policymaking by representing various sections of society,
thereby strengthening democratic participation and accountability.
(Source - NCERT Class X, Democratic Politics)

IV.	Our memories don’t all carry the same weight. Some moments settle into place without effort,
while others slip away almost immediately, leaving only the faintest trace behind. But what
pushes one experience toward long-term storage while another disappears? Is it the moment itself,
or the system deciding its fate?
A new study in Nature suggests the answer comes down to experience and timing. By examining
the hippocampus, thalamus, and cortex, researchers found that memories don’t become long-
lasting in a single step. Instead, they’re shaped by a cascade of molecular “timers” that activate
one after another, gradually determining which impressions consolidate into long-term memory.
This is a key revelation because it explains how we adjust the durability of memories. What we
choose to remember is a continuously evolving process rather than a one-time flipping of a switch.
For much of modern neuroscience, memory seemed straightforward. The hippocampus managed
short-term storage; with enough repetition or relevance, memories were thought to move into the
cortex and remain there. Existing models of memory in the brain involve transistor-like memory
molecules that act as on/off switches.

But that view couldn’t explain why some long-term memories fade quickly while others persist for
decades. In 2023, her lab identified a missing piece: a thalamic pathway that filters which
memories move toward long-term storage and routes them to the cortex. That raised a larger
question — once a memory leaves the hippocampus, what determines whether it sticks?
To track how memories mature, the researchers used a virtual-reality setup that let mice revisit
certain environments more often than others. This repetition created measurable differences in
how strongly each context was stored. The team then used a CRISPR-based approach to switch off
specific genes in the thalamus and cortex to test which molecular programs determine how long a
memory lasts. Their results revealed a stepwise sequence rather than a single mechanism.
Camtal, active early in the thalamus, stabilized new memories during their most vulnerable
stage. Tcf4, also in the thalamus, strengthened connections to the cortex as memories matured.
Ashll, a later-acting regulator in the cortex, triggered chromatin remodeling that helped convert a
fragile trace into something more durable. Disrupting any part of this sequence didn’t erase
memories — it simply caused them to fade sooner. Unless you promote memories onto these
timers, we believe you're primed to forget it quickly.
[Psychology; Word Count: 388]

brain-forgets-some-moments-but-holds-onto-others-48317

passages.GK-P0529: The constitutional role of the Governor at the state level has become a subject of intense judicial scrutiny. In a landmark case concerning bill assent delay, the Supreme Court interpreted the proviso of Article 200 of the Constitution. Under Article 200, when a Bill passed by a State Legislature is presented to the Governor, the Governor has four choices: declare assent, withhold assent, return the Bill with a message requesting reconsideration, or reserve the Bill for the President's consideration. The Court observed that if the Governor decides to withhold assent, the Governor must return the Bill 'as soon as possible' to the legislature. If the legislature passes the Bill again, with or without amendments, the Governor is constitutionally bound to give assent. The Court clarified that the Governor cannot permanently veto state legislation by simply declaring that assent is withheld without returning the Bill. This interpretation preserves the democratic structure by ensuring that the unelected constitutional head cannot overrule the elected legislature indefinitely.

IV.	When Pope Leo XIV announced that his first pastoral visit would be to Lebanon, the response
among many residents was marked by a mixture of anticipation and unease. The country, still
recovering from recent conflict and marked by a long history of sectarian violence, exists in a
state where the expectation of instability is deeply ingrained. Even periods of calm are often
perceived not as peace, but as temporary interruptions in an otherwise continuous cycle of
conflict.
Lebanon presents a paradox. It is widely regarded as a symbol of interreligious coexistence,
with political power formally distributed among different religious communities and physical
spaces reflecting this diversity. Mosques and churches stand in close proximity, and divisions
that once defined the city have, at least superficially, faded. Yet beneath this appearance of
unity lies a persistent anxiety shaped by historical memory and recurring violence.

The Pope’s visit, therefore, was not merely a religious event but also a symbolic gesture. It
brought attention to Lebanon’s role as both a site of coexistence and a locus of ongoing crisis.
While such visits are typically interpreted as affirmations of hope and renewal, in Lebanon
they carry an additional dimension: they momentarily suspend the anticipation of conflict
without necessarily altering its underlying causes.
This tension is further reflected in the everyday experiences of those living in the country.
Public expressions of welcome and unity coexist with the constant presence of military activity
and the awareness that stability may be fragile. Even as large gatherings celebrate messages
of peace, the sounds of conflict persist in the background, reinforcing a sense that normalcy is
provisional.
In this context, the idea of peace itself becomes ambiguous. It is not experienced as a stable
condition but as something deferred—an aspiration rather than a reality. The departure of
symbolic figures such as the Pope does not resolve this tension; rather, it often marks a return
to familiar uncertainties. Thus, Lebanon’s condition challenges conventional understandings of
peace, suggesting that in some contexts, peace may exist less as a state of being and more as a
momentary reprieve.
Source: Excerpt with edits - The Point Magazine, discussing Lebanon in the context of a papal
visit.

V. The Indian passport is a “travel document” and not a “citizenship document”, a senior official of the
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday (June 24, 2026). The purpose of the Indian passport is
to help Indians transit and travel through foreign ports and territories and it should not be compared with other
documents that are used to establish citizenship rights, the official said. A passport serves two functions: it
facilitates international travel and identifies the holder as it attests the holder’s nationality. Citizenship,
however, is a legal status defined exclusively under the Citizenship Act, 1955. The existence of a passport does
not, by itself, resolve all possible legal disputes regarding citizenship. The government’s position rests on a
technical but important distinction. A passport is evidence that the state accepted a claim of citizenship at the
time of issuance. It is not, however, a legal declaration that cannot be questioned under any circumstance.

community, largely residing in the Imphal Valley, and the Kuki-Zo tribal groups inhabiting the
hill districts. What began as tensions over identity and constitutional protections escalated into
one of the most severe internal security crises in the state’s recent history.
The immediate trigger for the violence was a solidarity march organised by tribal groups to protest
the Manipur government’s alleged move to grant Scheduled Tribe (ST) status to the Meitei
community. The Kuki-Zo groups opposed this proposal, fearing it would dilute existing affirmative
action benefits, affect land ownership rights in the hills, and weaken their political representation.
These long-standing issues relating to land, reservations, and power-sharing deepened mistrust
and led to widespread unrest.
The violence rapidly spread across the state, resulting in more than 250 deaths and the
displacement of nearly 60,000 people. Many displaced individuals continue to reside in relief
camps. The crisis was marked by repeated curfews, extended internet shutdowns, and persistent
instability, which effectively segregated communities and disrupted normal life across large parts
of Manipur.
As the unrest continued, then Chief Minister N. Biren Singh came under increasing criticism for
his inability to restore peace. Political instability intensified, and on February 9, 2025, after nearly

Assembly, he resigned Following this, President’s Rule was imposed, indicating a breakdown of
constitutional governance in the state.

VII. Delimitation is the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies to ensure
equal representation for equal populations. It is carried out to reflect changes in population as
recorded in the census, so that each constituency has, as far as possible, an equal number of
inhabitants. In India, delimitation is conducted by the Delimitation Commission of India, an
independent body whose decisions have the force of law and cannot ordinarily be challenged in
court. This process helps maintain fairness in the democratic system by ensuring that
representation in legislative bodies remains proportionate to population changes.
In India, delimitation is carried out based on the provisions of the Constitution of India and
the Delimitation Commission Acts enacted by Parliament. The number of seats allocated to
each state in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies is determined on the basis of
population figures from the census. However, to encourage population control measures, the
readjustment of seats has been frozen until after the first census conducted post-2026.
Delimitation plays a crucial role in strengthening representative democracy by ensuring
balanced political representation and equitable distribution of constituencies across the
country.

passages.GK-P0549: Parliament has passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026 to replace an Ordinance promulgated in May. The Bill changes section 2 of the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 by substituting 37 for 33 as the maximum number of judges other than the Chief Justice of India. The maximum sanctioned strength is therefore 38 when the CJI is included. Article 124(1) permits Parliament by law to prescribe this larger number; the Constitution itself need not be amended whenever the statutory ceiling changes. The Bill deems the change effective from 16 May 2026 and preserves steps already taken under the Ordinance. Its stated justification is the persistent gap between cases instituted and disposed of. On 1 January 2026, 92,101 cases were pending. During 2025, 75,410 fresh matters were instituted while 65,615 were disposed of. A larger court may also make it easier for the CJI to constitute benches of at least five judges for substantial constitutional questions under Article 145(3), without removing as many judges from regular benches. Yet sanctioned strength is only a ceiling. It does not itself fill vacancies, alter the appointments process, create regional benches, or guarantee that pendency will fall. Regional sittings remain governed by Article 130, under which the Court sits in Delhi or at another place appointed by the CJI with the President's approval.

IV.	Hantavirus is in the Hantaviridae family of viruses carried by rodents. The animals harbor the
virus without becoming ill, then shed it in their urine, droppings, and saliva. When those
secretions are disturbed—during cleaning, farming, or simply entering an infested space—the
virus can become aerosolized and inhaled by a nearby human. The virus can also infect
humans if they eat contaminated food, or touch a contaminated object and then their mouth.
More than 40 species of hantavirus exist in nature, and they’re broadly divided into two
categories—Old World and New World. Old World hantaviruses are endemic in Europe and
Asia and primarily cause bleeding disorders and kidney dysfunction. New World viruses are
more prevalent in the Americas and more commonly cause pulmonary edema, a condition in
which fluid accumulates in the lungs. The consequences of infection can be severe, especially
for infections with New World strains. Between 1 and 15 percent of infections lead to death in
Asia and Europe, but about half of hantavirus cases in the Americas are fatal.
Infections are not evenly distributed around the world. Between 10,000 to 100,000 hantavirus
infections are thought to occur each year, most of them in Asia and Europe. In the Americas,
only 150 to 300 infections are reported annually, with Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Bolivia
typically accounting for the majority. Between 15 to 50 cases are identified annually in the US.
The specific strain of hantavirus involved in a cluster of cases determines how deadly the
infections are likely to be. It also has important implications on how experts think the virus is
spreading, and what they must do to contain it. When hantaviruses make the jump from
animals into humans, it’s often in situations when contaminated urine, droppings, or nesting
materials of an infected rodent get stirred up—for example, when someone is sweeping out a
barn. However, people can also get infected with the virus when saliva, urine, or feces from an
infected rodent gets into skin wounds or into a person’s eyes, nose, or mouth. Most
hantaviruses are not spread between humans. It’s unclear why, although in one laboratory
study, the viruses appeared to produce very few mature virus particles in the lungs of infected
humans.

Article 19 and Reasonable Restrictions
Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression as a fundamental right;
however, Article 19(2) permits the state to impose reasonable restrictions on grounds including public order,
security of the state, and decency, creating a constitutional space for content regulation within defined limits.
The central legal challenge posed by the IT Rules amendments is determining whether regulatory measures remain
within the bounds of constitutional reasonableness or whether they encroach upon the core of the fundamental right
to free expression.

XI.	The United States and India have announced a framework for an Interim Agreement on reciprocal
and mutually beneficial trade. This agreement marks a significant step in strengthening economic
ties between the two countries and reinforces their commitment to the broader U.S.-India Bilateral
Trade Agreement (BTA) negotiations. The BTA talks were launched on February 13, 2025, by
President Donald J. Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The Interim Agreement is
described as a historic milestone that reflects a shared commitment to balanced and reciprocal
trade based on mutual interests and tangible outcomes.
The Interim Agreement lays the groundwork for deeper economic cooperation and aims to support
more resilient and diversified supply chains. It also seeks to address trade imbalances while
expanding market access opportunities for businesses in both countries.
Under the key terms of the framework, India has agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all U.S.
industrial goods. In addition, it will lower duties on a wide range of U.S. food and agricultural
products. These include dried distillers’ grains (DDGs), red sorghum used for animal feed, tree
nuts, fresh and processed fruits, soybean oil, wine and spirits, and other agricultural commodities.
This move is expected to provide significant market access for American exporters and enhance
agricultural trade between the two nations.
On the other side, the United States will apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18 percent on originating
goods from India under Executive Order 14257, issued on April 2, 2025. This order was designed to
regulate imports with a reciprocal tariff to address trade practices contributing to large and
persistent U.S. goods trade deficits. The 18 percent tariff will apply to a range of Indian exports,
including textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, plastic and rubber products, organic
chemicals, home décor, artisanal goods, and certain machinery.
However, the agreement also provides for the removal of reciprocal tariffs on a broad set of goods,
subject to the successful conclusion of the Interim Agreement. According to the Potential Tariff
Adjustments for Aligned Partners Annex under Executive Order 14346 of September 5, 2025, the
United States will eliminate tariffs on products such as generic pharmaceuticals, gems and
diamonds, and aircraft parts. These adjustments aim to promote aligned trade partnerships and
facilitate smoother trade flows in key sectors.
Overall, the Interim Agreement represents a strategic effort by both countries to deepen trade
relations, promote fairness, and create a more predictable and cooperative economic framework. It
sets the stage for further negotiations under the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement while
delivering immediate trade benefits and reinforcing the long-term partnership between the United
States and India

Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav chaired a high-level joint meeting of the National Tiger
Conservation Authority (NTCA) and the Project Elephant Steering Committee at the Sundarbans
Tiger Reserve. He emphasized that India’s conservation model must increasingly be science-driven
and supported by international collaboration, citing recent delegations from South Africa,
Namibia, and Botswana associated with the cheetah reintroduction programme.
Addressing the growing issue of human—wildlife conflict, Yadav outlined a three-pronged strategy
and announced a specialised initiative titled “Management of Tigers Outside Tiger Reserves.”
Officials also highlighted persistent challenges such as staff shortages, financial limitations, and
the urgent need to control invasive species that threaten wildlife habitats.
On elephant conservation, the Steering Committee reviewed progress on the All-India
Synchronized Elephant Estimation and DNA profiling of captive elephants. Particular focus was
placed on the Nilgiri Elephant Reserve and the Ripu—Chirang Elephant Reserve, along with
renewed attention on assessing elephant corridors and conflict-prone areas in the Bandhavgarh
region. www.lawpreptutorial.com

collision in Assam’s Hojai district, where seven elephants were killed after being hit by the

VIII. The Nazi regime made systematic and strategic use of language and media to advance its ideology
and consolidate public support. Official communications deliberately avoided direct words such as
“kill” or “murder,” replacing them with misleading and euphemistic terms that concealed the
reality of mass violence. Expressions like “special treatment,” “final solution” for Jews,
“euthanasia” for the disabled, and “selection” or “disinfection” were employed to normalise and
obscure acts of killing. Deportations to gas chambers were referred to as “evacuations,” while the
gas chambers themselves were labelled “disinfection areas” and designed to resemble bathrooms
with fake showerheads, further masking their true purpose.
Alongside this manipulation of language, the regime used media extensively to popularise its
worldview. Visual imagery, films, radio broadcasts, posters, slogans, and leaflets were used to
spread Nazi ideas and shape public opinion. Groups identified as enemies of the state were
stereotyped, mocked, and portrayed as dangerous or evil. Socialists and liberals were depicted as
weak and corrupt, while Jews were systematically dehumanised through propaganda, most
notably in films such as *The Eternal Jew*. These portrayals aimed to inflame emotions, redirect
public anger, and legitimise persecution of those labelled as “undesirable.”

IX.	The President of India has given assent to the Viksit Bharat—Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika
Mission (Gramin) (VB—G RAM G) Bill, 2025 marking a significant milestone in the
transformation of rural employment policy. Anchored in the principles of empowerment, growth,
convergence and saturation, the Act seeks to transform rural employment from a standalone
welfare intervention into an integrated instrument of development. It strengthens income security
for rural households, modernises governance and accountability, and links wage employment with
the creation of durable and productive rural assets, thereby laying the foundation for a prosperous
and resilient Bharat. All works are planned through a bottom-up process, and all assets created
are aggregated into the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack, ensuring convergence
of public investments, avoidance of fragmentation, and outcome-based planning aimed at
saturation of critical rural infrastructure, based on varying local needs. The Act reinforces the

right to demand employment while deepening decentralised, participatory governance. It
integrates transparent, rule-based funding, accountability mechanisms, technology-enabled
inclusion and convergence-driven development to ensure that rural employment not only provides
income security but also contributes to sustainable livelihoods, resilient assets and long-term rural
prosperity. The Act removes earlier dis-entitlement provisions and restores unemployment
allowance as a meaningful statutory safeguard. Where employment is not provided within the
stipulated period. The Act is implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, to be notified and
operationalised by the State Governments in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Funding is
provided through State-wise normative allocations based on objective parameters, ensuring
predictability, fiscal discipline, and sound planning, while fully preserving statutory entitlements
to employment.

passages.GK-P0593: The Lok Sabha has taken up three bills, namely the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, the Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 for consideration and passing. The three legislations are intended to increase the participation of women in the Lok Sabha and the assemblies of States and Union Territories. The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, popularly known as Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, provided for the reservation of nearly one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the legislative assemblies. The objective of the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam was to ensure greater participation of women in the democratic polity. These three bills have been brought to facilitate the delimitation of territorial constituencies and operationalise the provisions providing for the reservation of one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and legislative assemblies. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026, which has been introduced by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal in the Lower House today, is intended to increase the number of seats in the Lok Sabha from 543 to [1]. Out of [1] seats, 815 members will be elected from the States and 35 members from the Union territories. The objective of the bill is to implement one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha as well as the assemblies of States and Union Territories. Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam which was passed in 2023 provided that one-third reservation for women will come into effect after the delimitation exercise based on the first census after the commencement of the Act. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill 2026 states that the next census and the consequential delimitation exercise will take considerable time, thus restricting effective and dedicated participation of women in the democratic polity. The objective of the bill is to operationalise one-third reservation for women through delimitation exercise based on the latest published census.
