XXII. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced a new law that will prohibit social media
platforms from providing services to children under the age of 15. The measure is part of the
country's broader efforts to enhance online safety and protect minors from the potential risks
associated with social media use, including exposure to harmful content, cyberbullying,
privacy violations, and excessive screen time.
Under the new regulations, social media companies will be required to implement effective
and appropriate age-verification mechanisms to ensure that children below the age threshold
are unable to create or maintain accounts. Platforms must also actively monitor their services,
identify accounts belonging to underage users, and suspend or disable such accounts when
detected. The law places significant responsibility on digital platforms to ensure compliance
and prevent unauthorized access by children.
In addition to obligations on social media companies, the law imposes responsibilities on
regulators and caregivers. Regulatory authorities will oversee implementation and
enforcement, while parents and guardians are expected to play an active role in supervising
children's online activities and ensuring compliance with age restrictions.
The changes were announced through Cabinet Resolution No. 106 of 2026, which is expected
to come into force shortly after its publication in the Official Gazette. Once effective,

companies will be granted a 12-month compliance period to adapt their systems and processes
to meet the new legal requirements.
The UAE's move reflects a growing international trend toward stricter regulation of children's
access to social media In December 2025, Australia became the first
country in the world to ban social media use for individuals under the age of 16. The United
Kingdom has also indicated its intention to introduce a similar ban from spring 2027. Several
other countries, including France and Denmark, have proposed restrictions on social media
access for children under 15.
The new UAE law highlights increasing global concerns about the impact of digital platforms
on young users and demonstrates the willingness of governments to adopt stronger regulatory
measures to create a safer online environment for children.

passages.GK-P0596: India imports most of the crude oil it consumes, leaving its economy exposed to price increases and disruptions along maritime supply routes. Offshore basins may contain domestic oil and gas, but exploration is uncertain and costly: seismic data can identify prospects without proving that a commercially recoverable discovery exists, and a deepwater exploratory well can cost around ₹1,000–1,200 crore. On 1 August 2026, the Union government announced Cabinet approval of the ₹84,084 crore National Offshore Exploration Scheme, known as Samudra Manthan. Earlier reporting on the proposal described government risk-sharing for exploratory drilling and seismic surveys, alongside the auction of deepwater blocks. The final legal and financial obligations, however, must come from the notified scheme and exploration contracts. Constitutionally, Article 297 vests valuable resources beneath India’s territorial waters, continental shelf, and exclusive economic zone in the Union. Parliament’s Union List also assigns regulation and development of oilfields and mineral oil resources to the Union field. Samudra Manthan therefore combines economic policy, maritime geography, statutory licensing, public expenditure, and environmental oversight.

X.	The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) is India's primary legislation for dealing
with unlawful activities, terrorism, and threats to the sovereignty and integrity of the country.
Enacted in 1967, the Act was originally designed to prevent activities that threatened India's
unity and territorial integrity. Over the years, particularly through amendments in 2004,
2008, 2012, and 2019, it has evolved into the country's principal anti-terrorism law.
Under the UAPA, the government has the power to declare organisations as unlawful or
terrorist organizations and to take legal action against individuals involved in terrorist
activities. The 2019 amendment further expanded these powers by allowing the government to

designate individuals, and not just organisations, as terrorists. The Act also provides special
provisions for investigation, arrest, detention, and prosecution in terrorism-related cases.
Supporters of the UAPA argue that it is an essential tool for combating terrorism, insurgency,
and organised extremist activities that threaten national security. They contend that the law
enables security agencies to investigate complex terror networks and prevent attacks.
However, the Act has also been the subject of significant debate and criticism. Critics argue
that some provisions, particularly those related to arrest, detention, and bail, can potentially
affect civil liberties and may be vulnerable to misuse. As a result, the UAPA remains an
important yet controversial component of India's legal framework, reflecting the ongoing
challenge of balancing national security concerns with the protection of individual rights and
democratic freedoms.

X.	The resignation of Justice Verma became a notable event in India’s judicial history and
sparked widespread debate on judicial accountability. Justice Verma, a senior judge of the
higher judiciary, resigned following allegations of misconduct that raised concerns about
ethical standards in the judiciary. The controversy led to strong public and institutional
scrutiny, with demands for transparency and a fair inquiry process.
The episode highlighted the challenge of balancing judicial independence with accountability
mechanisms. While internal procedures were initiated to examine the allegations, the case
exposed gaps in how complaints against judges are handled. Justice Verma’s resignation was
seen as an important moment that prevented a deeper institutional crisis but also left behind
questions about reform.
Overall, the incident became a reference point in discussions on strengthening judicial ethics
and ensuring public trust in the justice system.

VI.	The country’s 7th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity shows progress in
forest cover and ecosystem restoration, assessing progress towards global biodiversity goals set
for 2030. India reports gains in forest cover, ecosystem restoration and some species recovery,
including tigers and rhinos. However, land degradation, data gaps and limited conservation
coverage remain major challenges for meeting biodiversity commitments.
The report is the country’s official submission under the CBD, an international environmental
treaty through which nations commit to conserving biological diversity and using natural
resources sustainably. All parties to the convention are required to submit periodic reports
outlining what actions they have taken, what progress they have achieved and what
challenges remain.

India is one of the world’s megadiverse countries, with ecosystems ranging from the
Himalayan mountains to coastal mangroves and tropical forests, underlining the importance
of the report. Its biodiversity performance has a substantial influence on global outcomes.
Data from the report will feed into international assessments examining whether the world is
on track to meet biodiversity commitments and identifying any gaps in monitoring systems
and governance that could affect long-term conservation efforts. However, the report also
highlights significant challenges. Monitoring biodiversity is complex and expensive, and
several new indicators still lack standardised protocols. Different ministries collect data at
varying intervals, while rapid improvements in satellite technology can make comparisons
across years difficult. These factors can affect the consistency of datasets and the long-term
comparability of trends. The report provided a broad picture of policy alignment, measurable
progress, data trends and gaps in India’s biodiversity strategy. [Word Count: 258]

The 6-3 majority comprised Chief Justice John Roberts (who authored the opinion) along with conservative Justices
Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett—both Trump appointees from his first term—and the three liberal Justices
Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
The three dissenting justices were conservatives Clarence Thomas, Brett Kavanaugh, and Samuel Alito; Kavanaugh
was also appointed by Trump during his first term.
The liberal justices did not join the part of the majority opinion invoking the "major questions doctrine"; that
portion was authored by Roberts and joined only by the conservative majority members who voted against the
tariffs.

Core Legal Reasoning of the Majority

impose tariffs, stating: the court's task was to decide "only whether the power to 'regulate ... importation,' as granted
to the president in IEEPA, embraces the power to impose tariffs—it does not".
Roberts invoked the major questions doctrine, a conservative legal principle requiring that executive actions of "vast

passages.GK-P0643: The Karnataka Government will approach the Supreme Court seeking permission to implement the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) for the 2026-27 financial year and question the taking away of the Right to Work enshrined in the Constitution by implementing the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G) Act. Law and Parliamentary Affairs minister H K Patil told a news conference that the state would seek directions from the apex court to "allow us to have an action plan for this year and implement that". "Whatever was in existence under NREGA is to be facilitated for the state," Patil said. The decision was taken during the Karnataka Cabinet meeting held Thursday. MGNREGA was repealed by the Centre when it passed the VB-G RAM G Act in December 2025. Karnataka has opposed the move and passed a resolution against the decision in the Assembly during the joint session of the legislature held in January this year. Karnataka is among the states opposing the VB-G RAM G Act, calling it anti-federal and financially burdensome. The state has argued that the new law unfairly shifts costs to states by requiring them to bear 40 per cent of the expenditure, unlike the earlier system under which the Centre funded beneficiaries' wages.
passages.GK-P0644:
XIX. Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently concluded a significant five-nation diplomatic tour
aimed at strengthening India's strategic, economic, technological, and energy partnerships
with key countries across Europe and West Asia The tour reflected India's growing global
engagement and its efforts to deepen cooperation with important international partners amid
evolving geopolitical challenges.
During the visit, Prime Minister Modi travelled to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Italy,
Sweden, Norway, and the Netherlands. The UAE leg of the visit was particularly important
due to concerns regarding global energy security and instability in the Middle East.
Discussions focused on strengthening bilateral trade, investment, energy cooperation, and
regional stability.

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
In Italy, the Prime Minister held high-level discussions on trade, clean energy, innovation,
defense cooperation, and connectivity initiatives. The visit also emphasized collaboration in
emerging technologies and sustainable development. Italy remains one of India's important
partners within the European Union.www.lptedtech.com
The visits to Sweden and Norway highlighted cooperation in green technology, climate action,
renewable energy, innovation, digital transformation, and maritime affairs. Nordic countries
are recognized globally for their leadership in sustainability and technological innovation,
making them valuable partners for India's development goals.

IX.	The Padma Awards are among the highest civilian honours conferred by the Government of
India. Instituted in 1954, these awards recognise exceptional achievements and distinguished
service in various fields, including art, literature, education, sports, medicine, science,
engineering, social work, public affairs, and civil service. The Padma Awards are announced
annually on the eve of Republic Day and are presented by the Government of India at a
ceremonial function held at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
The awards are divided into three categories: Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, and Padma
Shri. The Padma Vibhushan is awarded for exceptional and distinguished service of the
highest order, while the Padma Bhushan recognises distinguished service of a high order. The
Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian award in India, is given for distinguished service in
any field. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The selection process involves recommendations from the public and various institutions,
which are examined by a Padma Awards Committee. The committee's recommendations are
then submitted to the Prime Minister and the President for approval.
Over the years, the Padma Awards have honoured a wide range of individuals, including
scientists, artists, athletes, social reformers, and public servants. By recognising outstanding
contributions to society, the awards celebrate excellence, inspire public service, and highlight
the diverse achievements that contribute to India's cultural, social, and national development.
passages.GK-P0722: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) permeates critical sectors, sovereign regulation has moved from the periphery to the centre of state policy. At the India-AI Impact Summit 2026, the government unveiled the 'MANAV' (Moral, Accountable, National Sovereignty, Accessible, Valid) framework, outlining the nation’s official AI governance doctrine. Unlike Western models that focus heavily on existential risks, or market-driven approaches that prioritize corporate speed, the Indian approach explicitly ties AI safety to developmental goals. The doctrine highlights compute equity, suggesting that global compute resources should not be monopolized by a handful of tech conglomerates. In tandem, the summit saw the release of Param2, a 17-billion parameter indigenous Multilingual Large Multimodal Model designed to support 22 official languages. By providing free open-access datasets via the newly established 'AIKosh' repository, the state aims to encourage local developers to build localized applications. However, critics point out that public compute availability remains bottlenecked, and the legislative interface between automated profiling and the DPDP Act 2023 remains unresolved.

passages.GK-P0726:
XVIII. The NASA Artemis II mission, scheduled to launch no earlier than April 1, 2026, will mark a
historic milestone in human space exploration. It will be the first crewed mission of NASA’s
Artemis program and the first time humans travel beyond low-Earth orbit since the Apollo era
If successful, it will send astronauts near the Moon for the first time in more than 50 years,
following the last lunar mission, Apollo 17.
The four-member crew consists of Reid Wiseman (Commander), Victor Glover (Pilot),
Christina Koch (Mission Specialist), and Jeremy Hansen. The mission is significant not only
for its exploration goals but also for its diversity milestones. Glover will become the first
person of color to travel on a lunar trajectory, Koch the first woman, and Hansen the first non-
U.S. citizen to journey toward the Moon.
Artemis II will use NASA’s powerful Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and the Orion crew
capsule. After launch, the SLS will propel Orion into space and place it on a free-return
trajectory around the Moon. This trajectory allows the spacecraft to loop around the far side of
the Moon and return to Earth primarily under the influence of gravity, minimizing fuel
requirements and enhancing mission safety.
During the mission, Orion is expected to travel approximately 7,500 kilometers beyond the
Moon’s surface at its farthest point. The astronauts will not land on the Moon but will conduct
tests of the spacecraft’s systems, navigation, communications, and life-support capabilities in
deep space. These tests are essential before future Artemis missions attempt lunar landings.
The entire journey will last a little over a week. After completing its flyby of the Moon, Orion
will return to Earth and splash down in the Pacific Ocean. The mission serves as a critical
stepping stone toward future crewed lunar landings under the Artemis program and NASA’s
long-term objective of establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon and eventually
preparing for human missions to Mars.
Source: https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/artemis-ii-the-international-space-race-
and-what-is-at-stake-for-the-us/article 70806797.ece

Global Satellite Navigation Systems
The world’s principal satellite-navigation systems include four global systems GPS of the United States, GLONASS of
Russia, Galileo of the European Union, and BeiDou of China and two important regional systems NavIC of India and
QZSS of Japan. 
GPS (Global Positioning System) is operated by the United States. Its first NAVSTAR/GPS satellite was launched
in 1978. The United States is committed to maintaining at least 24 operational satellites, and the official GPS
portal states that the U.S. Space Force has been flying 31 operational satellites for well over a decade.
GLONASS (Global Navigation Satellite System) is operated by Russia. Flight testing began with the launch of the
first satellite in October 1982. The system is built around a 24-satellite operational constellation, and the official
GLONASS status page recorded 28 satellites in constellation, of which 24 were in operation, on 30 March 2026. 
Galileo is the European Union’s civilian global navigation system. Its first launch took place on 21 October 2011.
ESA states that the Galileo space segment is designed as a 30-satellite constellation, including 27 active satellites
and 3 spares. The current Galileo service-status page also shows that the latest satellites, GSAT0233 and
GSAT0234, were still under commissioning in March 2026 after their December 2025 launch.

passages.GK-P0728:
IV.	Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, thought that if we are distressed about
something external, “the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it; and this you
have the power to revoke at any moment.”
I love this, but also know from experience that finding that power can be near impossible at times.
We can’t just click our fingers and be rid of, say, grief, or the stress of work, or health worries.
When we are lost in the forest, our fear might not be directly caused by the forest, or our being lost
in said forest, but while we are actively lost in the forest it very much feels like the source of our
fear is being lost in the forest.
But it is helpful to remember that our perspective is our world. And our external circumstances
don’t need to change in order for our perspective to change. And the forests we find ourselves in
are metaphorical, and sometimes we are unable to escape them, but with a change of perspective
we can live among the trees.
Source: Power - The Comfort Book

passages.GK-P0730:
VII. Once a mystical substance, ethanol’s journey to a well-understood chemical involved many
cultures, alchemists, botanists, chemists and biologists over centuries. The discovery that
linked biology to chemistry was Louis Pasteur’s demonstration that living yeast cells are
responsible for the fermentation of sugar into alcohol in the absence of oxygen. Today, crops
like beet, sugarcane and maize are the main sources of ethanol.
Ethanol has multiple uses: as an antiseptic, in medical wipes and hand sanitisers; to dissolve
many medicines that do not mix well with water; and in liquid pain medications, cough and
cold medicines. It helps keep medicines mixed and stable and also acts as a preservative. It is
also used in mouthwashes, perfumes, deodorants, paints, and markers
As a fuel and fuel additive, it has a 200-year history. In 1826, American inventor Samuel
Morey developed an engine that ran on ethanol and turpentine. In 1860, Nicholas Otto, a
German engineer best known for developing the modern internal combustion engine, used
ethanol as the fuel in one of his engines. In 1896, Henry Ford built his first automobile, the
quadricycle, to run on pure ethanol. In 1908, he produced the flexible fuel Model T that could
run on ethanol, gasoline, or a combination of both. Ethanol was also an important fuel for early
rockets and is still used in some lightweight rocket-powered aircraft.
The demand for ethanol, which World War I drove, decreased with the arrival of cheap crude.
In the 1970s, the ban on export of petroleum to countries that supported Israel during the Yom
Kippur war by oil-producing Arab nations ensured ethanol a permanent place in the fuel mix.
Brazil, the world leader, has at least 25% ethanol blended fuel, and special “flex-fuel” cars run
on pure ethanol or a mix. In 2021, Ford launched the world’s first hybrid electric flex-fuel
vehicle that can operate on a battery and E85 (fuel with 85% ethanol).
In 2024, the first commercial ethanol-to-aviation fuel facility began operations in the [C].
India, with its rich sugarcane production, started blending 5% ethanol in petrol in the early
2000s. Today, we are at 20%. While E20-ready vehicles are being rolled out, millions of older
vehicles cannot handle this mix. The idea of growing your own fuel is tempting, even more so
for a country like India. But we need to take into account the issue of engine technology and
the reality of a water-intensive crop like sugarcane in a water-starved country.

passages.GK-P0814: The administration of Waqf properties in India sits at the intersection of religious freedoms, property law, and secular state governance. Under Article 26 of the Constitution, religious denominations enjoy the right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes and manage their own affairs in matters of religion. However, property management remains subject to state regulation under public order, morality, and health. The Waqf Act 1995 established State Waqf Boards and the Central Waqf Council as statutory bodies to oversee dedicated properties. Following the 44th Constitutional Amendment of 1978, the right to property ceased to be a Fundamental Right under Article 31 and became a constitutional right under Article 300A.
passages.GK-P0815:
VII. Over the past decade, China and India have shown sharply divergent trajectories in tackling air
pollution. Once infamous for its smog, Beijing reduced its annual PM2.5 levels by more than 50%
between 2013 and 2021, whereas Delhi continues to rank among the world’s most polluted cities.
Beijing’s clean-air transformation resulted from a multifaceted, top-down approach anchored in
coherent policy, strict enforcement, and regional coordination. Key interventions included the Air
Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan and the Blue Sky Protection Campaign, which
targeted energy, transport, and industry. The government expanded electric mobility, shut down
or relocated polluting industries, replaced coal-fired boilers with natural gas, imposed China VI
vehicular emission standards, and built a dense PM2.5 real-time monitoring system with
substantial penalties for non-compliance. Coordination with neighbouring Tianjin-Hebei provinces
through a unified ‘airshed’ strategy ensured that transboundary pollution was effectively
regulated. These measures drove PM2.5 levels down from 102 pg/m* in 2013 to 31 pg/m* in 2024.
India, by contrast, has a strong statutory framework for environmental protection, including the
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment Protection Act, 1986, and
rules covering waste, construction, and emissions. Initiatives such as the National Clean Air
Programme, Graded Response Action Plan, odd-even vehicle rationing, and the Commission for
Air Quality Management (CAQM) exist, yet they are largely reactive and fragmented. Multiple
agencies—from the Union government to municipal bodies—function in silos, slowing decision-
making, weakening enforcement, and diffusing accountability. Pollution control boards are
chronically underfunded and understaffed, and regional coordination, particularly to tackle
stubble burning, remains ineffective.
China’s success also stems from sustained investment in clean energy, electric mobility, and
industrial relocation, whereas Delhi’s attempts, such as the Bawana project and waste-to-energy
plants, have faltered. Delhi’s pollution is compounded by industrial and vehicular emissions,
construction dust, open waste burning, and meteorological inversions. Public transport expansion
and behavioral change have lagged, and temporary measures like odd-even rationing have limited
long-term impact.
For India to achieve meaningful improvement, it need not replicate China’s political system but
can adopt key principles: long-term, mission-oriented governance treating air pollution as a public
health emergency; accelerated clean-energy transition; enforceable transport reforms including
BS-VI compliance, EV infrastructure, and public transport expansion; functional industrial
relocation with monitoring; and regional coordination akin to Beijing’s airshed model for the
Delhi-NCR region.
Source — The Hindu article dated 224 December, 2025

passages.GK-P0817: The legal landscape surrounding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has entered a crucial phase before international judicial bodies. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague has been called upon to examine both provisional measures applications under the 1948 Genocide Convention and advisory requests regarding the legal consequences of prolonged occupation. Under international humanitarian law, particularly the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949, occupying powers are strictly prohibited from transferring parts of their own civilian population into occupied territory. India has consistently advocated for a negotiated Two-State solution, recognizing Palestine in 1988 while maintaining strong bilateral ties with Israel.

India's Objections to the IFD Agreement
India's foundational objection is that investment facilitation constitutes a non-mandated, non-multilateral issue: the
WTO was established to regulate trade in goods, services, and intellectual property, and expanding its mandate to
govern FDI without a unanimous multilateral decision violates the spirit and text of the Marrakesh Agreement.
India views the plurilateral route being used to advance the IFD as a structural threat to the WTO's consensus-based,
member-driven character, arguing that allowing groups of willing members to move ahead on specific issues
without the agreement of the full membership effectively creates a two-tier WTO dominated by major economies, in
which issues of particular importance to developing countries and LDCs can be bypassed.
New Delhi has warned that if plurilateral agreements are normalised within the WTO framework, powerful
economies could use the same mechanism to target domains affecting developing countries such as agricultural
subsidies and domestic support without requiring the participation or consent of those directly affected.

passages.GK-P0892:
GENERAL KNOWLEDGE

I. THREE bills moved together through Parliament in August 2025, and taken separately, each
look almost technical. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirtieth Amendment) Bill, 2025
deals with what happens to a chief minister or prime minister who is arrested. The Jammu and
Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025 and the Government of Union Territories
(Amendment) Bill, 2025 extend a similar logic to other Union Territories. But critics across the
opposition and among constitutional scholars argue that re ad together, the three bills amount to
something far larger than routine housekeeping legislation: a rewiring of how elected
governments in India can be removed from office, and by whom. At the heart of all three bills is
a single mechanism. If a prime minister, a chief minister, or a minister is arrested and held in
custody for 30 consecutive days on a charge that carries a prison term of five years or more, that
person is required to resign. If they don't, the office is deemed vacant automatically. No
conviction is required. No chargesheet needs to have been filed. No court needs to have
examined the evidence at all.

IX.	The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, initially emerged as a platform for dialogue
between educated Indian elites and the British colonial administration. In its early phase, the
Congress relied on constitutional methods such as petitions, resolutions, and appeals, reflecting
the belief that political progress could be achieved through gradual reforms within the colonial
framework. This approach was shaped by the socio-political context of the time, where mass
political mobilization was neither feasible nor widely accepted
However, the limitations of this moderate strategy became increasingly evident in the early
twentieth century. The failure of the British government to respond meaningfully to Indian
demands, combined with economic hardships and racial discrimination, led to growing
disillusionment among nationalist leaders. As a result, the Congress gradually transformed its

methods and objectives, incorporating mass participation and more assertive forms of protest. This
shift marked a significant change in the nature of the nationalist movement—from elite
negotiation to popular mobilization.
The entry of Mahatma Gandhi into the Congress further altered its character. By emphasizing
non-violence and mass participation, Gandhi enabled the Congress to reach peasants, workers, and
marginalized groups, thereby broadening its social base. Movements such as Non-Cooperation and
Civil Disobedience reflected this new strategy, which sought to challenge colonial authority by
undermining its moral and administrative legitimacy rather than relying solely on constitutional
agitation.
Despite internal disagreements and periodic setbacks, the Congress remained the central force of
the Indian freedom struggle. Its ability to adapt to changing political circumstances, balance
ideological differences, and integrate diverse social interests allowed it to sustain relevance over
decades. The evolution of the Indian National Congress thus illustrates how nationalist
movements often reshape their strategies in response to political realities, rather than following a
fixed ideological path.
Source: Themes in Indian History — Part II “Colonialism and the Countryside / The Nationalist
Movement”)

Article 368 of the Constitution governs the procedure for constitutional amendments, requiring both a majority of
the total membership of the House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting; amendments affecting
federal provisions additionally require ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.

Article 81 dictates the principle of equal representation, providing that the ratio between a state's allocated seats
and its population must be broadly uniform across all states, with exceptions only for states with populations below
six million.

architecture, with the former halting the inter-state reallocation of seats and the latter extending the freeze until the

Right to Strike in India
The right to strike refers to the collective refusal by workers to perform their duties in order to demand better
wages, working conditions, or labour practices, and is broadly recognised across political systems as a
legitimate, though last-resort, instrument of collective action.
In India, while the right to protest is guaranteed as a fundamental right under Article 19 of the Constitution, the
right to strike is not a fundamental right but a statutory legal right subject to regulatory restrictions; it flows
from the fundamental right to form associations and may be subjected to reasonable restrictions imposed by
the state.
The right to strike received limited recognition under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and was subsequently
regulated under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, both of which have now been subsumed under the Industrial
Relations Code, 2020.
At the international level, the right to strike is recognised under the conventions of the International Labour
Organization (ILO), of which India is a founding member, establishing an international normative framework
against which domestic restrictions on strike action may be assessed.
Constitutional Foundations of Labour Law in India
The Preamble to the Constitution enshrines values of justice, liberty, equality, and dignity, which together form the
moral foundation for labour legislation in India; while not directly enforceable in courts, the Preamble guides the
interpretation of labour laws in favour of worker protection and social equity.

VI.	International Women’s Day (IWD) is an annual global celebration that aims to educate society
on the remarkable women’s rights movement. This day marks a call to action for accelerating
gender parity, highlighting the ongoing efforts for continued advocacy and action worldwide,
and celebrating the cultural, political, and socio-economic achievements of women and girls.
It provides a global platform for collective action and collaboration in campaigning for women’s
rights and empowerment, breaking down barriers for women and girls all around the world.
The theme for International Women's Day intends to promote generosity and collaboration,
highlighting how reciprocal support creates more opportunities for women, as mentioned on
the IWD official website. Several demonstrations in demand of women’s franchise and political
rights of “proletarian” women or women workers have preceded Women's Day.
In the early twentieth century, the garments industry was the single largest employer of
women. However, the working women had to grapple with poor working conditions, long work
hours, and paltry wages. Most of these garment workers were engaged in an internal
subcontracting system that made extensive use of homework and marked their positions in the
production cycle as learners but not “skilled” labourers, thus they received meagre wages
compared to semi-skilled male operators. Their work hours were as long as 75 hours a week
and they were in some cases even required to supply their basic materials such as needles and
threads. They were fined for being late at work, and during their working hours, they were
locked up inside the workshop to stop them from taking breaks.

IV.	The garden had belonged to the Chowdhury family for seven generations, a small plot of earth in
Mumbai where jasmine vines climbed white walls and crows nested in the old neem tree. Maya
returned to it after fifteen years of living abroad, expecting nostalgia. Instead, she found
bewilderment. Everything was smaller than she remembered—the garden she had imagined as
vast now seemed confined, almost suffocating in its smallness. Her grandfather sat in the
courtyard as he always had, though age had rendered him nearly unrecognizable. His hands, once
strong enough to coax blooms from stubborn soil, trembled as he tended the plants. He did not
acknowledge her arrival; perhaps he did not recognize her. Maya wandered through the garden,
touching the familiar plants, and noticed something strange: the flowers were blooming in the
wrong season, their colors muted and peculiar. The gardener, old Ranjit, spoke to her in hushed
tones that evening. He told her that her grandfather had not spoken a word in three years, that he
spent every night under the neem tree, whispering to the darkness. Ranjit believed the garden
was dying, that something fundamental had shifted in the earth itself. When Maya finally
approached her grandfather to embrace him, he recoiled. As she stood there, rejected and
bewildered, she understood that she had lost not just the garden of her childhood but the
grandfather she thought she knew.
Source: The Secret Garden; Novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett

VII. The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, commonly known as the Quad, is an informal strategic
grouping comprising four countries: India, the United States, Japan, and Australia. The
initiative was first proposed in 2006 and established in 2007 and was revived in 2017 amid
growing concerns about security, economic stability, and freedom of navigation in the Indo-
Pacific region.
The Quad aims to promote a free, open, inclusive, and rules-based Indo-Pacific.
Although it is not a formal military alliance, the four countries cooperate on a wide range of
issues, including maritime security, disaster relief, climate change, critical and emerging
technologies, cybersecurity, infrastructure development, supply-chain resilience, and public

worldwide economic depression. Agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after
1930. As the demand for agricultural goods fell and exports declined, peasants found it
difficult to sell their harvests and pay their revenue. By 1930, the countryside was in turmoil.

VIII. Anyone who has navigated parenthood in the contemporary era will readily attest that childrearing
has become inextricably entwined with perpetual digital consultation, and it is precisely this
phenomenon that Simon Rogers — data editor at Google and former journalist — endeavours to
chronicle in What We Ask Google, an ambitious if ultimately constrained attempt to distil two
decades of anonymised search queries into what the subtitle optimistically characterises as "a
surprisingly hopeful picture of humankind." Drawing upon Google Trends data extending as far
back as 2004, Rogers assembles a thematically organised compendium of collective human
curiosity, ranging from the delightfully mundane — the perennial supremacy of burrito-folding
queries over trouser-folding, disrupted only fleetingly by a 2019 Marie Kondo Netflix phenomenon
— to the intermittently poignant, treating search behaviour as a sociological mirror capable of
reflecting something genuine and substantive about human nature. Certain trends resist all
rational elucidation: why Austrians, Nigerians, and Canadians disproportionately query nocturnal
back pain, or why Kansans most frequently solicit Google's orthographic assistance with "chaos"
while their Missourian neighbours are most confounded by "unconscious," remains entirely opaque.
Where contextual scaffolding is available, Rogers deploys it effectively — noting, for instance, that
early 2023 witnessed search interest in parental caregiving overtaking child-related queries, a
telling demographic testament to the mounting pressures upon the so-called "sandwich
generation." The book's most arresting visual — a cartographic rendering of the 2024 solar eclipse's
trajectory, overlaid with regional spikes in searches pairing "eyes" and "hurt" — speaks eloquently
to the intellectual limitations of certain searchers. However, the work is fundamentally
compromised by its conspicuous omissions and its author's institutional allegiances: Rogers, who
migrated to Google from Twitter in 2015, offers a conspicuously rose-tinted appraisal of the
corporation's broader societal footprint, providing negligible acknowledgment of artificial
intelligence's seismic disruption of search behaviour, the cascading economic devastation inflicted
upon digital publishers by Al-generated summaries, or the considerable role that Silicon Valley's
technological apparatus has played in amplifying the very parental anxieties he catalogues with
such apparent sympathy. The complete absence of any engagement with political search behaviour,
Donald Trump, or humankind's demonstrably darker digital impulses further exposes the selective
nature of Rogers' curation. His interpretive generosity occasionally collapses into naivety — most
egregiously when he frames the high frequency of plasma donation queries as altruistic impulse
rather than as damning evidence of the grotesque socioeconomic inequities endemic to the
American healthcare system. What remains is a diverting, if editorially circumscribed, aperture
onto collective human preoccupation — suitable bathroom reading, though one should approach its
optimistic conclusions with considerable scepticism.

Article 21 and Personal Liberty
The protection under Article 21 is available to “persons”, which includes citizens as well as non-citizens.
The Article operates primarily as a limitation on the State, meaning deprivation of life or personal liberty must have
legal authority and follow the prescribed procedure.
The phrase “procedure established by law” means a deprivation can occur only through a procedure laid down in a
valid law.
Article 21 is enforceable through constitutional remedies, and a person can approach the Supreme Court under
Article 32 or a High Court under Article 226 for its protection.
The Supreme Court has held that the procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just, and reasonable, and not arbitrary
(as developed in constitutional jurisprudence).
Article 21 has been interpreted to include the right to live with human dignity, and not merely a physical or animal
existence (as recognised in Supreme Court jurisprudence).
Article 21 has been interpreted to include procedural safeguards in matters involving arrest, detention, and criminal
justice, alongside protections in Article 22 and related laws.
Article 21 has been judicially expanded to cover several rights treated as part of “life” and “personal liberty,” such as
the right to privacy (recognised as a fundamental right through Supreme Court interpretation).
Article 21 is part of Part III (Fundamental Rights) and is among the most frequently invoked provisions in
constitutional litigation because it applies broadly to State action affecting life and liberty.

VII. The Indus Valley Civilisation, also known as the Harappan Civilisation, was one of the world's
earliest and most advanced urban civilisations. It flourished between approximately 2600 BCE
and 1900 BCE in the northwestern regions of the Indian subcontinent, covering parts of
present-day India and Pakistan. The civilisation was named after the city of Harappa, where
its remains were first discovered in the 1920s.
The Indus Valley Civilisation is renowned for its well-planned cities, advanced drainage
systems, standardised weights and measures, and impressive craftsmanship. Major urban
centres included Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, and Lothal. The streets were laid out ina
grid pattern, and most houses had access to drainage facilities, reflecting remarkable urban
planning.
Agriculture formed the economic foundation of the civilisation, while trade connected it with
distant regions such as Mesopotamia. The Harappans produced pottery, beads, seals, and
metal objects of high quality. One of the enduring mysteries of the civilisation is its script,
which remains undeciphered.
Around 1900 BCE, the civilisation gradually declined, possibly due to environmental changes,
shifting river systems, and economic disruptions. Despite its decline, the Indus Valley
Civilisation remains a landmark in human history and a testament to early urban
development and cultural achievement.

VI. The mathematical equations governing black holes existed as immutable truths long before such
cosmic phenomena themselves came into being — a proposition that cleaves directly through one of
philosophy's most contentious fault lines: the nature of mathematics itself. Staunch Platonists
contend that mathematical structures, from foundational axioms to elegant geometric constructs
like the tetrahedron, possess an existence wholly independent of human cognition, constituting not
merely a descriptive language of humanity's own fabrication, but rather the very ontological
substrate upon which reality is constructed. Their adversaries, however, vehemently assert that
mathematics is an exclusively anthropogenic enterprise — a sophisticated intellectual scaffolding
imposed upon a universe that would remain utterly indifferent to its absence. Sergiu Klainerman,
distinguished professor of mathematics at Princeton University, positions himself unequivocally
within the former tradition, maintaining that mathematical truth antedates human consciousness,
and that the mathematician's vocation is fundamentally one of excavation rather than invention.
His monumental contributions — including landmark proofs establishing the stability of vacuous
space and the structural resilience of black holes under perturbation — represent, in his firm
conviction, discoveries of pre-existing eternal verities rather than intellectual constructions. To
conflate the invented instruments of mathematical inquiry with the discovered truths they
illuminate constitutes, for Klainerman, a categorical error of profound epistemic consequence. Born
and raised in Communist Romania, Klainerman gravitated toward mathematics during his
undergraduate studies at the University of Bucharest in 1969, drawn not merely by prodigious
aptitude but by something considerably more existential: in a society saturated with ideological
coercion, mathematics alone offered an inviolable sanctuary of pure, uncompromising truth,
entirely beyond the authoritarian reach of Nicolae Ceausescu's regime. This philosophical
conviction was not cultivated in academic discourse but forged through lived experience — a young
man who had witnessed a totalitarian state attempt to subjugate truth itself, discovering in one
discipline an absolute that no political apparatus could manipulate. Dissatisfied with his
university's prevailing pedagogical orthodoxy — which demanded rote assimilation of technical
knowledge while perpetually deferring genuine conceptual understanding — Klainerman sought
intellectual nourishment through an informal study group led by the promising mathematician
Otto Liess, where he encountered partial differential equations: the mathematical language
describing the continuous transformation of physical phenomena across space and time, from
thermal conduction to the evolution of gravitational fields. These sessions, though imperfect in

their own right, proved irrevocably decisive, inaugurating his lifelong immersion in the analytical
framework that would ultimately underpin his celebrated investigations into shock waves, spatial
stability, and black hole dynamics. Yet Klainerman's intellectual ascent unfolded against the
suffocating constraints of life under totalitarianism — constraints compounded considerably by his
Jewish identity, which had already systematically circumscribed his father's distinguished medical
career and now threatened to extinguish his own scholarly ambitions entirely.

passages.GK-P0981: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act is a regulation built around differentiated risk. It prohibits certain practices, places extensive controls on high-risk systems, regulates general-purpose AI models, and imposes transparency duties on specified uses. The Regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024, but its obligations were deliberately phased. Rules on prohibited practices began to apply in February 2025, while governance and general-purpose-model duties followed in August 2025. On 2 August 2026, Article 50 transparency duties became applicable. These include informing people when they interact directly with certain AI systems and identifying specified AI-generated or manipulated content. Deployers must also disclose deepfakes and some AI-generated public-interest content. The AI Office simultaneously obtained enforcement powers concerning general-purpose AI models. However, a 2026 amendment postponed major obligations for Annex III high-risk systems until December 2027 and for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products until August 2028. The Act may reach providers outside the EU when they place covered technology on the EU market or when output produced by the system is used in the EU. Thus, the 2026 milestone combines transparency, market access, institutional enforcement, and fundamental-rights protection without making every provision applicable on the same day.

IV.	Many Years Later as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia was to remember
that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice. At that time Macondo was a
village of twenty adobe houses, built on the bank of a river of clear water that ran along a bed
of polished stones, which were white and enormous, like prehistoric eggs. The world was so
recent that many things lacked names, and in order to indicate them it was necessary to point.
Every year during the month of March a family of ragged gypsies would set up their tents near
the village, and with a great uproar of pipes and kettledrums they would display new
inventions. First they brought the magnet. A heavy gypsy with an untamed beard and sparrow
hands, who introduced himself as Melquiades, put on a bold public demonstration of what he
himself called the eighth wonder of the learned alchemists of Macedonia. He went from house
to house dragging two metal ingots and everybody was amazed to see pots, pans, tongs, and
braziers tumble down from their places and beams creak from the desperation of nails and
screws trying to emerge, and even objects that had been lost for a long time appeared from
where they had been searched for most and went dragging along in turbulent confusion behind
Melquiades’ magical irons. “Things have a life of their own,” the gypsy proclaimed with a harsh
accent. “It’s simply a matter of waking up their souls.” José Arcadio Buendia, whose unbridled
imagination always went beyond the genius of nature and even beyond miracles and magic,
thought that it would be possible to make use of that useless invention to extract gold from the
bowels of the earth. Melquiades, who was an honest man, warned him: “It won’t work for that.”
But José Arcadio Buendia at that time did not believe in the honesty of gypsies, so he traded
his mule and a pair of goats for the two magnetized ingots. Ursula Iguaran, his wife, who
relied on those animals to increase their poor domestic holdings, was unable to dissuade him.
“Very soon we'll have gold, enough and more to pave the floors of the house,” her husband
replied. For several months he worked hard to demonstrate the truth of his idea. He explored
every inch of the region, even the riverbed, dragging the two iron ingots along and reciting
Melquiades’ incantation aloud. [Word Count: 407]

consumption, such as salaries.

economy, including business investments in factories and government infrastructure like roads and bridges.

population size, distribution, age structure, literacy, occupation, housing conditions, and other
socio-economic indicators. Governments conduct censuses periodically to obtain accurate and
reliable data for effective policy-making, resource allocation, and development planning. The
information gathered through a census is essential for determining electoral representation,
planning welfare schemes, improving public services, and monitoring population trends.
In countries like India, the census plays a vital role in shaping governance and developmental
strategies. Conducted under the provisions of the Census Act, 1948, it serves as the foundation
for policies related to health, education, employment, and infrastructure. Reliable census data
helps governments identify regional disparities and address the needs of different sections of
society. Thus, the census is an indispensable tool for evidence-based governance and socio-
economic planning.

V. Supreme Court’s lament about the government not willing to modernise the delivery of the death
sentence – it was hearing a petition to replace death by hanging with lethal injection – needs some
parsing, and continuous discussions beyond cases in court. The death penalty has three debates that run
concurrently. First, whether capital punishment should be abolished. Second, a restrained and diligent
application of the penalty. SC and CJIs have time and again appealed to HCs to be ultra-careful when


sentencing convicts to death. The sentencing itself is harrowing for most convicts, however hardened
the criminal. On death row, it is long years of appeals till death is delivered or the sentence commuted.
The third debate is on the ‘best’ – or ‘humane’ – way to service the sentence.
Neither the debates nor the arguments are new. A British govt commission report in the 1950s exploring
modes of execution said of its goal: any method untried that would inflict death as painless and certain
as hanging but with “greater decency” and without the “degrading and barbarous association with which
hanging is tainted”. The argument against this debate is that there’s no ‘humane’ way; the very decision
is troubling. That discussing ‘best methods’ is in fact, an attempt to protect shared values – the natural
right to life and ‘dignity of death’. The reality, though, is that so long as the death penalty is on the
statute, it must be asked: is hanging the most certain, quickest, and least painful method with minimum
bruising? Should there be options? If so, what?
No method is ‘best’. The world recoiled when Alabama last year used nitrogen gas asphyxia in a global
first as a new mode, claiming death would be instant. Instead, the convict struggled for life for several
minutes – nitrogen was on for 15 minutes. US prisons are exploring new ways because drugs for lethal
injections (sodium thiopental) are difficult to source – countries are ceasing manufacture and banning
export of drugs for capital punishment. US states have re-introduced electrocution and the gas chamber
(hydrogen cyanide). Finding trained personnel is a challenge. Non-medical people carrying out a
medical mode of execution have also seen botched executions. India on its part has a shortage of
hangmen although executions are rare – there can be no worse torture than a botched hanging. To that
end, SC’s point on GOI’s lack of response is on point. It is not alone about policy. It’s a complicated
medico-legal issue. However squeamish it makes one, the question of option is not to be sidestepped.


SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/death-by-2/

V. Large and intensely black; thick, velvety fur; has a faint fringe of white hair across his chest;
not easy to find in ordinary light.” When his daughter Clara’s beloved black cat Bambino
disappeared while she was convalescing in a sanatorium, Mark Twain put out the ad in the
New York American and spent days receiving strangers with abandoned black cats in the hope
of finding Bambino among them. The cat returned on his own, but it was no secret in New York
that the American writer loved his daughter, and Bambino, with equal fervour.

That they occupy a special place in the lives of their humans is no secret. But separated by
centuries and continents, the spurt in litigation and mediations in India’s capital over pets and
strays only goes to show that the law is just beginning to catch up with what the heart has
always known: That animals matter — not as assets, but as companions. And, in some
circumstances, they are the bone of contention or caught between adversaries. Take, for
instance, a civil suit filed in 2023 by an advocate against his neighbours in south Delhi. The
reason: Their pet had chased him, leading him to fall and fracture his wrists. When TMC MP
Mahua Moitra broke up with lawyer Jai Anant Dehadrai, the bitterness spilled over into a
custody tussle over their beloved Rottweiler, Henry.

It may seem trivial to some, absurd even, but these disputes, at their core, are declarations of
how much trust is conveyed through a wag of a tail or the flick of a feline ear. In lonely, crowded
urban metropolises, pets provide the kind of unstinting comfort that few can. Neighbours fight,
lovers part, but what lingers is the bond with the creature left in between. Reforms to Australian
law last month recognised this: For the first time, in cases of separation, Australian courts will
factor in emotional attachment when determining pet ownership. As Delhi courts navigate this
tricky terrain, it is a reminder that love, no matter how small or furry, always leaves a trail.

V. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has rightly stressed the need to make a distinction between
refugees and infiltrators. Although valid, the problem lies in the application of objective
parameters by those in power to draw distinctions. Even where proper policy and a legal
framework exist, issues may arise. Also at play is the level of official understanding. In India,
which is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol, there is
no comprehensive single law defining who a refugee is, leaving scope for arbitrary action. Till
the end of March 2025, apart from the Citizenship Act 1955 and the Passports Act 1967, three
laws (the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 and the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920) were applied to deal with foreign nationals, including refuge
seekers. From April, the Immigration and Foreigners Act replaced the three pre-Independence
laws and subsumed the Immigration (Carriers’ Liability) Act, 2000. While this streamlined the
legal framework, the absence of a refugee policy document has also led to different yardsticks
for the refugee community in India. While there was a rehabilitation policy in 2014 for about
63,000 Tibetan refugees, there is no such document for the nearly 90,000 Sri Lankan Tamils.
At the end of June 2023, the population of refugees or persons of concern in India was over
2.11 lakh (also counting those from Myanmar, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Africa and West Asia).
Any undocumented or overstaying refugee is regarded as an illegal migrant (Citizenship Act).
He can also be called an infiltrator. Thus, genuine and harmless refugees risk facing
harassment.
Even though the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was aimed at providing citizenship to six
religious minorities belonging to Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan, it drew sharp criticism
as it discriminated on the lines of religion and left out sections of Muslims, and also Sri Lankan


Tamils and the Rohingya, both minorities in their countries. But in a notification last month,
undocumented or overstaying Tamil refugees, who have registered themselves with the
authorities, were granted exemption from penal provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners
Act, provided they took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. Other groups, too have
been covered. Still, there is no change in the recent trend of religion-based exclusions. There
is nothing fundamentally wrong with the approach of discreet humanitarian relief to refugees
in general but this has to be backed by consistent, rational and fair treatment for all.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/refugees-and-infiltrators-on-different-
yardsticks-for-indias-refugee-community/article70167639.ece

V. Were it not for the tragic circumstances of his death, Y Puran Kumar would have been
seen as an example of social mobility and of the upholding of the Indian Constitution’s
promise of equality. He was a Scheduled Caste (SC) Indian Police Service officer of the
Haryana cadre; his wife, Amneet P Kumar, is an SC IAS officer, and his brother-in-law is an
MLA in Punjab. On the face of it, Kumar and his family had reached the upper echelons of
government and politics. His suicide and the eight-page note he leaves behind, which alleges
systemic discrimination, including by senior IPS officers, however, casts a shadow on that
image. It also raises disturbing questions about entrenched biases that cramp and distort
institutional spaces. These questions must be addressed, not evaded.

The allegations of “mental and administrative torture” and “caste-based discrimination,
public humiliation, targeted mental harassment and atrocities” by senior officers in Haryana
in Kumar’s dying declaration must be probed. The National Commission for Scheduled
Castes (NCSC) has directed the Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, Chandigarh,
to submit an action taken report in seven days. The state government and police must
investigate Kumar’s suicide urgently, in a transparent manner. The temptation to close ranks
in the face of public and judicial scrutiny must be avoided. Issues of embedded prejudice and
discrimination and their effect on the mental health of those at the receiving end are too
important to be brushed under the carpet. This must be a moment for the police to reflect and
introspect.

Caste is a proven fact in crime and punishment in India. The Status of Policing in India
Report (2025) by Common Cause and Lokniti found that victims of torture are “most often
from marginalised communities” and that police personnel across states see certain SC and
ST communities as “criminal”. The survey also found that “one in every four Scheduled
Caste (SC) police personnel think that Dalits do not get justice”. The caste-based, and even
casteist, nature of policing in India is an unfortunate remnant of a colonial structure that
urgently needs to be consigned to the past. Doing so, however, is easier said than done, and
requires police forces — particularly at the leadership level — to be open and sensitive as
they turn the searchlight inwards. Kumar’s death and his allegations must not be swept under
the institutional carpet. The Haryana police cannot allow discrimination to go unchecked and


unpunished within.

the global norm, the manner in which the India-U.K. economic relationship is unfolding is
a refreshing change. U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s two-day visit to India last week
reinforced the existing solidity in economic relations and deepened them. India’s
negotiations with the U.S. have been fraught, erratic, and dramatic. U.S. President Donald
Trump has also shown that he is more than willing to change the contours of deals already
struck. Negotiations with the European Union have been less fraught and dramatic, but
there certainly seems to be a gap between the positive assurances made by the leaders and
what the negotiators say in private about the deal’s progress. Against this backdrop, Sir
Starmer chose to bring a delegation of more than 100 entrepreneurs, cultural
representatives, and university vice-chancellors and left India with defence, investment
and movie deals, further cementing the trade deal signed in July. The keenness to deepen
trade relations makes eminent sense. India, despite being the fourth-largest economy in the
world and one of the largest markets, accounts for less than 2% of the U.K.’s total
merchandise exports. The U.K. accounts for about 3% of India’s exports. There is ample
scope for trade to grow. Growing India-U.K. trade could also mitigate some of the impact
of the U.S.’s punitive 50% tariffs, if they remain.

One of the unsaid reasons why India is slowing its capital expenditure is because it needs
to fund its defence acquisitions. Sir Starmer’s visit made sure that some of these
acquisitions — in the form of a £350 million missile supply deal — came the U.K.’s way.
The U.K. government also revealed that 64 Indian companies have so far committed to

PASSAGE 5
A surplus monsoon bodes well for agriculture and rural demand this year. GST reforms, which
kicked in 10 days ago, are also expected to spur consumption. So, RBI’s revised growth
forecast of 6.8% isn’t surprising. It seems like a small increment from 6.5%, but in a $4tn
economy each fraction of a percentage point amounts to billions of dollars. Yet, it’s nothing to
celebrate when Trump’s tariffs have cast a shadow over roughly $50bn worth of goods
exports.

Even otherwise, 6.5% or 6.8% isn’t an aspirational growth rate for India. As the finance ministry
has said more than once this year, India needs to grow at 8% “every year, at least for a
decade” to become a developed country by 2047. Yes, India remains the fastest growing major
economy, but relative performance doesn’t improve living standards. In the late 1990s, when
India’s population was growing at 2% per annum, economists recommended a 9% growth
target for 7% effective growth – to double income every 10 years. Now, although population
growth has slowed to about 1% per year – based on estimates in the absence of a census –
8% is the slowest acceptable GDP growth target. However, a new Morgan Stanley analysis
shows even 8% might be too slow. To address the growing problem of unemployment, the
asking rate must be 12.2%, it says. The report points to record youth unemployment – 17.6%
– and a surge in agricultural employment, which are faces of the same coin. Growing farm
employment is in fact the clearest sign of a jobs crisis. As countries develop, agriculture’s
share in employment and output shrinks. Farm work accounts for only 1.2% of employment in
US. But in India, this year’s Economic Survey showed agriculture’s share in employment
increased from 44.1% in 2017-18 to 46.1% in 2023-24.

Over the next 10 years, 84mn Indians – equal to the population of Germany – will hit working
age. So, creating good jobs for them has to be a national priority. Long-neglected
manufacturing, whose share in GDP had slipped to 15.9% in 2023-24 from 16.7% in 2013-14,
should be the preferred engine for this, because it creates more related jobs than services.
That’s how US built its middle class in the 1950s, and China in the 2000s. The vision of
developed India hinges on this.

questions.questionText: Oceanic Nifio Index (ONI) is used to measure
options: Wind speed in the Indian Ocean
questions.solution: The Oceanic Nifo Index (ONI) measures the departure (anomaly) of Sea Surface Temperature (SST) from the long-term average in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean (Nifio 3.4 region). If SST is +0.5°C or more for several months —> El Nifio If SST is —0.5°C or less > La Nifia It does not directly measure air pressure, wind speed, or monsoon strength — though these can be affected by El Nifio/La Nifia conditions.

questions.questionText:
Under which of the following constitutional provisions are the grounds for disqualification of a
person for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament specified?
questions.solution: Article 102 of the Constitution of India specifies the grounds on which a person can be disqualified from being chosen as, and from being, a member of either House of Parliament. questions.questionText: VB G-Ram G changes guaranteed days of employment per year from -

questions.solution: One of the greatest mysteries of the Indus Valley Civilisation is its undeciphered script, which remains unread despite decades of research by archaeologists, linguists, and historians. 1. It shares its border with five Indian states.
2. The total length of its border with India is approximately 1751 km.
8. It shares its border with the Indian states of Sikkim, West Bengal, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh
and Uttarakhand.
4. Nepal shares a border with Assam.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: The question is about Nepal and its border with India. Statement 1: Correct — Nepal shares its border with 5 Indian states.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the India—UK Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain
Observatory:
I. It was announced during the India—UK Prime Ministers’ bilateral engagement in October
2025.
II. It was created only to regulate domestic coal mining auctions in India.
III. It was formalised through a Research Collaboration Agreement signed in March 2026.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statement I is correct because the initiative was announced during the India-UK Prime Ministers’ bilateral engagement in October 2025. Statement III is also correct because it was later formalised through a Research Collaboration Agreement signed in March 2026.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about formats and tournaments in international cricket:
I. Test cricket is the traditional form of the game played over five days with two innings for
each team.
II. The T20 World Cup tournament started in 2007 and was earlier known as the World T20.
III. The T20 World Cup tournament is organised every year for both men and women teams.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statements I and II are correct. Test cricket is the traditional and longest format of international cricket and is played over five days with two innings for each team.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the International Olympic Committee:
1. It was established in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin and Demetrios Vikelas.
2. Its headquarters is located in Lausanne.
8. Its current President is Kirsty Coventry and Director General is Christophe De Kepper.
4. Its official motto is “Citius, Altius, Fortius — Communiter” meaning “Faster, Higher,
Stronger — Together”.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.solution: 1. International Olympic Committee founded in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin & Demetrios Vikelas.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about Ladakh as a testbed for human spaceflight missions:
I. The low temperatures, hypoxia, and isolation in Ladakh are analogous to spaceflight
conditions.
II. Ladakh experiences sub-zero temperatures for over six months, low precipitation, low
moisture, and largely cloudless conditions.
II. Ladakh receives high humidity and frequent rainfall, making it suitable for simulating
tropical climate conditions.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statements I and II are correct because Ladakh’s extreme environmental conditions, including low temperatures, hypoxia, and isolation, closely resemble certain aspects of spaceflight environments. Its prolonged sub-zero climate, minimal precipitation, low humidity, and clear skies make it an effective natural testbed for human spaceflight preparation.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Strategic Plan for Tuberculosis
Elimination:
1. The National Strategic Plan for Tuberculosis Elimination aims to eliminate tuberculosis in
India five years ahead of the global target.
2. targets an 80% reduction in TB incidence and 90% reduction in TB mortality by 2025.
3. The plan was launched for the period 2020-2030 under the World Health Organization.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because the National Strategic Plan for TB Elimination was launched by the Government of India for the period 2017— 2025, not 2020-2030, and it is India’s domestic roadmap, though aligned with global TB elimination goals.

questions.questionText:
Which constitutional doctrine would most likely be examined by courts while reviewing a
social media ban for minors in India?
questions.solution: + The Doctrine of Proportionality is used by courts to determine whether a restriction on a Fundamental Right is necessary, reasonable, and proportionate to the objective sought. + If India were to impose a social media ban for minors, courts would examine whether the restriction is proportionate to the goal of protecting children.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements based on recent SIPRI findings on India’s arms imports:
1. India was the 2nd largest arms importer during 2021-2025 with about 8.2% share.
2. Russia’s arms exports declined by around 64%, reducing its global share to about 6.8%.
8. India’s top three arms suppliers were Russia, France, and Israel.
4. France was India’s largest arms supplier during this period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.solution: Short Explanation: 1. India = 2nd largest importer (~8.2%).

questions.questionText:
Which of the following statements best reflects the outcome of the Hunter Committee inquiry
and the Congress response in December 1919?
options:
The Hunter Committee held Dyer guilty of mistaken duty, removed him from command,
and the Congress session at Amritsar demanded a fully responsible government in India.

The Hunter Committee cleared Dyer of wrongdoing, restored his command in service, and
the Congress session at Amritsar demanded only limited police reforms in Punjab.

The Hunter Committee postponed action against Dyer for further review, retained him in
office, and the Congress session at Amritsar supported gradual reforms under British
supervision.

The Hunter Committee recommended lenient treatment for Dyer without retirement, and
the Congress session at Amritsar avoided political demands and focused only on local
administrative grievances.
questions.solution: is correct because it accurately combines both developments described here. The Hunter Committee held Brigadier-General Dyer guilty of acting under a mistaken notion of duty, which resulted in his removal from command and premature retirement from the army.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:
1. India hosts populations of all seven species covered by the IBCA.
2. The cheetah became extinct in India before being reintroduced through a conservation
programme.
8. India's leadership in launching IBCA reflects its growing role in global biodiversity
governance.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: India does not host all seven big cats (Jaguar and Puma are native to the Americas). However, the cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952 and later reintroduced, and the launch of IBCA strengthens India's position in global wildlife conservation diplomacy.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding recent developments in social media regulation:
1. Australia became the first country to enact a nationwide social media ban for children
under 16 years.
2. The UAE became the first Arab country to prescribe a minimum age for social media use.
3. Karnataka has debated introducing restrictions on social media access for children below
16 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
options:
1,2 and3

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
questions.solution: + Australia became the first country to enact a nationwide social media ban for children under 16 years. The United Arab Emirates became the first Arab country to prescribe a minimum age (15 years) for social media use In India, Karnataka has debated introducing restrictions on social media access for children below 16 years, drawing inspiration from international developments.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the Census in India:

Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India.

8. The Census in India provides data for the delimitation of constituencies but has no role in
the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution: 1. Incorrect — Census is listed under Entry 69, not Enumeration 67, in the Union List of the Constitution of India.

questions.questionText:

questions.solution: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to 1, 3 and 4 only. Therefore option B is the answer identified by the official key.

questions.questionText:

questions.questionText:

maritime cooperation.
III. India and the ROK adopted a Comprehensive Framework for Partnership on Shipbuilding,
Shipping and Maritime Logistics.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution: Statements I and III are correct because India’s Maritime Amrit Kaal vision is linked with new opportunities for long-term and strategic cooperation with the ROK. The two sides also adopted a Comprehensive Framework for Partnership on Shipbuilding, Shipping and Maritime Logistics.

questions.questionText:

questions.questionText:
With reference to the evolution of Census operations in India, consider the following
statements:

out during the tenure of Lord Ripon.
2. The first regular synchronous Census of India in 1881 was conducted under Lord Mayo.

Census Act, 1948 after Independence.

questions.solution: 1. Incorrect — The first non-synchronous population count in India was carried out during the tenure of Lord Mayo, not Lord Ripon.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional issues examined in the
Sabarimala Temple judgment:
1. The Supreme Court of India examined whether the restriction on women’s entry was
protected as an essential religious practice under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution of
India.
2. The Court held that the restriction did not violate Articles 14 and 15, since denominational
rights take precedence over equality rights.
8. The judgment involved balancing freedom of religion with constitutional guarantees of
equality and non-discrimination.

questions.solution: 1. Correct — The Court examined whether the exclusion of women was an essential religious practice protected under Articles 25 and 26.

questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional and electoral framework of
Nepal:

questions.solution: Statement 1 Correct Statement 2 Incorrect — Only 165 members are elected via FPTP; the remaining 110 are elected through Proportional Representation Statement 3 Correct — Nepal uses a mixed electoral system, making this a subtle but important point

Ill. The agreement grants India operational control of the Shahid Beheshti terminal at

questions.solution: All three statements are correct. India and Iran signed a 10-year agreement to strengthen long-term cooperation at Chabahar Port, replacing the earlier short-term one-year arrangement.
